Examinations to determine whether all individuals from a sample are required to be back-calculated and the effects of Rosa Lee Phenomenon (RLP) on the growth parameter estimates produced when only the oldest individuals from a sample are back-calculated, has not been undertaken. This study investigated the need to back-calculated all individuals from a sample and the effects of RLP on the precision and accuracy of growth parameter estimates produced when only back- calculating the oldest individuals from the sample. To analyse this, datasets of four shark species – the blue (Prionace glauca), oceanic whitetip (Carcharhinus longimanus), creek whaler (C. fitzroyensis) and Australian blackspot sharks (C. coatesi) – were used. Sub-setted datasets for each species were fit to von Bertalanffy, Logistic and Gompertz growth functions. Maximum likelihood ratio test was used to determine if there was a significant difference between growth parameter estimates produced by sub-setted datasets and the full dataset. Results showed that precise and accurate model fit can be achieved when sub-setted datasets are fit to best fit growth models for oceanic whitetip, creek whaler and Australian blackspot sharks. In addition, the life history of a species influenced the effects of RLP on produced growth parameter estimates. This study provides an insight into the need to back-calculate all individuals from the sample. Further, the findings highlight the bias introduced due to RLP on the growth parameter estimates produced when only back-calculating the oldest individuals from the sample.

6605: The effects of fishing-capture stress extend beyond immediate and delayed death, because discarded animals that are released back into the environment experience long-term, growth, behavioural, energetic and reproductive impairments. Reproductive consequences can impair adults’ ability to contribute to the increase in population abundance and neonate survival and performance and need to be thoroughly investigated. Nevertheless, despite being one of the most threatened vertebrate group, data on the reproductive consequences of fishing-capture stress for chondrichthyans are virtually non-existent. This lack of data jeopardizes the assessment of the real consequences of fishery practices and the development of effective fisheries management measures. We investigated whether trawling capture and air exposure experienced by near-term, pregnant females affects neonatal traits in the southern fiddler ray Trygonorrhina dumerilii, a viviparous ray commonly caught as bycatch in southern Australian recreational and commercial fisheries. We measured neonatal growth rate, yolk-sac consumption rate, swimming performance, burying and boldness behaviour. Results highlighted that, compared to control neonates, neonates born from mothers subjected to trawling simulation had smaller yolk-sac reserves and a slower consumption rate of these energy resources, that is likely the cause of the observed reduced growth rate. These neonates also showed lowered boldness and, when a predator attack was simulated, swam for shorter distances and showed a different burying response. A slower growth rate might expose neonates to higher predation risk, and similarly, the altered burying and swimming behaviour may reduce their ability to escape from predators. A lowered boldness, by reducing the area explored and the ability to obtain food and resources, might reduce neonates’ competitive ability. Further research is needed to investigate the real consequences of the observed alterations in a natural environment, but these first data suggest a possible reduction in neonates’ survival rate that can ultimately have severe consequences for recruitment and population abundance.

6606: Hammerhead sharks (Sphyrnidae) are iconic and charismatic species that have been well studied in the northern hemisphere and received little attention until more recently in Australian waters. The general aim of this project was to provide a better understanding of the scalloped hammerhead shark (Sphyrna lewini) in Queensland, Australia to improve conservation and management strategies. Multiple methodologies were used to determine (i) the distribution of suitable habitat for juvenile sharks and overlap with marine protected areas; (ii) fine-scale movement of juvenile sharks within these habitats and determine behavioural states using high-resolution acoustic tracking; (iii) thermal tolerance range “thermal niche” of hammerhead sharks using historical catch records from the QSCP; and (iv) isotopic overlap between hammerhead sharks and with other co-existing large sharks. Species distribution modelling identified highly suitable areas occurring around highly developed areas, such as Moreton Bay, Hervey Bay, Townsville, Cairns, and the Gold Coast. These habitats occurred within low protection zones or outside of MPAs. Two diving patterns were observed, and the two-state behavioural modelling uncovered two activity states, which were influenced by distance to seagrass, coral habitats, and habitat depth. Quantile regression modelling determined catches of hammerhead sharks in relation to changes in seas surface temperatures, catches in the southern areas were most likely to occur between 20℃ - 25℃ and likely to occur throughout the year in the northern areas. Scalloped hammerheads showed a wider δ 13 C and lower δ 15 N than the more specialised great hammerhead. In summary, these results provide new information and highlight the relevance of movement and habitat use information in the conservation and management of endangered iconic shark species.

6607: Within the Indo-Pacific, there is mounting concern for the conservation status of elasmobranchs primarily due to fisheries pressure, but also degradation of habitat. These threats are generally concentrated inshore and consequently, species of large-bodied elasmobranchs that require access to shallow coastal or riverine environments during their life history have experienced drastic population declines. The four Indo-Pacific sawfish (Pristidae) and three river shark (Glyphis) species epitomize the extinction risk of large-bodied elasmobranchs in this region. A large factor in the high incidence of extinction risk in sawfishes and river sharks is their similar life history strategies which compounds their exposure to both non-marine (freshwater and estuarine environments) and marine environmental and anthropogenic pressures. Northern Australia is presently the only nation where viable populations of all Indo-Pacific sawfish species, and G. garricki and G. glyphis are known to persist. However, rebuilding of sawfish and river shark populations cannot rely on refuges within northern Australia alone. There is a need to document the status of populations in other nations where these species may be persisting so that effective local conservation measures can be developed and implemented. Recently, there has been increased interest in Papua New Guinea (PNG) as a possible refuge for Indo-Pacific sawfish and river shark species. This presentation will detail findings from surveys carried out during 2017-2020 in remote regions of PNG. These surveys aimed to document the distribution and threats to sawfish and river sharks through observations of small-scale fishers, fisher questionnaire surveys, and catch enumeration by local fishers. Our findings indicate that sawfish species Anoxypristis cuspidata, Pristis clavata, Pristis pristis and river shark species G. garricki and G. glyphis are found throughout southern PNG, however the recent emergence of dried swim bladder market (high value product in Asia), and a lack of local fisheries management threatens these species.

6608: The whale shark Rhincodon typus is the world’s largest extant species of fish, and aggregates normally to capitalize on foraging opportunities. The species’ predictable occurrence at certain sites globally have made them a considerable attraction for marine wildlife tourism. In Oslob, Philippines, the whale shark tourism operation uses daily feeding to allow tourists to have close, near-shore interactions with the sharks. The sharks have now been visited by 1 million tourists since 2012 -- making Oslob as world’s largest non-captive whale shark tourism destination. Here, we used 8-year longitudinal data of their daily presence in Oslob to assess seasonality, abundance and population dynamics of the aggregation. Through photoidentification, we identified 428 individual whale sharks between March 31, 2012 and December 31, 2019, with 300 males, 82 females, and 44 of unknown sex, with a mean total length of 4.93 ± 1.29 m, consistently juvenile male-biased like most other coastal aggregations globally. Unlike most aggregations globally, the sharks in Oslob occur daily, year-round, with a maximum of 38 individuals seen in a single day, and a minimum of 1. Individual P-403, first identified on June 10, 2012, was the individual that most frequented the site (1,697 out of 2742 days), while 20% of the aggregation were only sighted once. A total of 87 sharks were also resighted in other places in the Philippines, with one matched to Malaysia, highlighting their highly mobile nature. Scars were observed in 35% of the aggregation which emphasizes the need to improve local and national legislation for their protection. Although some extended or year-round occurrence has been documented in places like Tanzania and the Maldives, the predictability in Oslob is unique highlighting the impacts of provisioning activities on this Endangered species. Assessing long-term fluctuations in abundance and behaviour at the individual and population levels are imperative.

6609: The Global Finprint project has spent the last few years carrying out baited remote underwater video stations at more than 370 reefs in 58 nations making it the most comprehensive study of coral reef sharks and rays. The results demonstrate that as a group reef sharks have declined dramatically. At least 20% of reefs surveyed had no reef sharks recorded, and this group is believed to be ecologically extinct in these areas. The use of MPAs, fishing controls and improved governance were demonstrated to provide pathways to improve reef shark status. Using data for individual species, and accounting for coral reef area in the nations surveyed we were able to demonstrate that declines in reef sharks has led to increased extinction risk for species in both the IndoPacific and Atlantic oceans, with most species likely to qualify for Vulnerable or Endangered categories of the IUCN Red List. The response of coral reef ray populations has been more complex with the loss of sharks leading to increases in the abundance of small rays such as mask and lagoon rays in some locations. However, in many locations rays were also not observed. However, these rays may not yet meet criteria for listing in threatened categories of the IUCN Red List. The global Finprint study has provided a unique window into the world of sharks and rays that live on coral reefs, providing evidence of concerning declines but also avenues to achieve conservation success.
6610: Negative shark-human interactions are relatively unpredictable and ungovernable events. These events draw significant media attention and historically have elicited emotionally driven public perceptions of sharks. Governments and communities globally have developed extensive shark safety guidelines intended to minimize public risk with sharks. However, expert workshops and community outreach suggested that communities may not strictly adhere to the advice presented. Scientists and communities alike have also indicated they wish to learn the scientific evidence substantiating such guidelines to inform individual risk assessments. This review assessed the scientific basis of safety guidelines intended to minimise shark bite risk. Current literature on shark ecology and behaviour was compared with 36 shark safety guidelines identified from six global governments with high shark bite incidence. Each guideline was ranked for the level of scientific veracity according to the likely accuracy, amount of supporting evidence, and overall congruency between species and locations. Guidelines fell into two broad categories: (1) advice aiming to reduce risk by modifying human behaviour, and (2) advice based on knowledge of shark behaviour and ecology. Most of the more universally presented guidelines like “swim, surf, snorkel, or dive with a buddy,” “swim in clear water,” or “minimize splashing and noise,” were assessed to have limited basis in current scientific knowledge about shark behaviour and ecology, but instead should be considered as general water safety advice. Meanwhile, guidelines primarily associated with predator-prey interactions and ecological knowledge of shark behaviour within specific regions had the strongest scientific basis. It is recommended that general guidelines should be reframed as general safety precautions for beachgoers. Furthermore, development of more specific shark safety guidelines tailored towards local shark behaviour and ecology is recommended to provide more effective advice at reducing shark bite risk.

6611: The rapid increase in development, marketing, and implementation of shark bite- mitigation measures have led to a rise in peer-reviewed studies independently assessing the efficacy of mitigation measures. Yet, the lack of standard methods to test such measures and the diverse approaches and reporting characteristics of the tests prohibit direct comparison of different mitigation strategies. We did a literature review to summarise previous testing and reporting of mitigation-measure efficacy, and develop and recommend a framework for future testing. We reviewed and assessed 93 papers following the systematic-review protocol PRISMA: 46 papers testing personal protection products, 44 papers testing area-mitigation strategies, and 3 papers testing personal protective equipment. Experimental design, sample size, and variables recorded varied extensively among studies and type of mitigation measures. Interpretation of results and determination of whether a strategy should be considered valid was also inconsistent among studies. We provide a standard testing and reporting framework, and suggest an optimal experimental design, including power analyses, to determine sample size, most-relevant variables, appropriate statistical tests, and a new terminology to report the efficacy of mitigation strategies (i.e., ‘efficient’ ≥ 70% reduction in shark-bite risk; ‘promising’ 50–70% reduction in risk). Using this framework will allow direct comparison of different mitigation measures, which will also enable policy makers and consumers to make informed decisions when selecting and implementing the most appropriate measures for the intended outcome.

6612: A quarter of sharks and rays are threatened with an elevated risk of extinction, largely as a result of overfishing. Fortunately, rising awareness of the plight of sharks and rays has driven a recent increase in conservation actions. Despite this progress, there is concern that limited resources are being allocated appropriately to ensure these actions translate into conservation outcomes, such as halting declines and reducing extinction risk. Further, signatories to the Convention on Biological Diversity are required to deliver the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity by 2020 and hit targets that will ensure, sustainable fisheries (Target 6) and extinctions are avoided (Target 12), and the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals to ‘conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources’ (Target 14). Yet there are few marine indicators to track these global targets. We describe the first results of a global reassessment of the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species status of all 1,238 Chondrichthyans involving 99 assessors spanning 10 regional and thematic workshops in 2018–2020 and more than 600 time series from 200 species. We develop indices of global change in abundance and extinction risk to track these global targets, and outline the first of these indices for oceanic sharks and rays.

Although this has brought economic benefits to local communities, the impact on the sharks themselves has been side-lined. Poor compliance to local guidelines or codes of conduct, can potentially have negative impacts on the sharks, which may threaten the sustainability of the industry as a socio-economic provider. Between February 2013 and March 2020, in-water surveys were conducted to understand the potential impacts of tourism on the whale sharks in Pintuyan, Southern Leyte, Philippines. Here, a community-run, small-scale operation has been active since 2006. We used mixed-effects models and generalized linear models to determine variables affecting interaction duration and predictors of avoidance behaviour. In total, 1,902 in-water human-shark interactions were recorded with 220 individual whale sharks, over an 8-year time span with yearly seasonal data collection. Avoidance behaviour was documented on 29% of interactions, with a mean in-water interaction duration of 7 min 54 seconds ± 9 min. Swimmers were observed within 4 m and 20 m of the shark on 67% and 92% of interactions respectively. Motorboats were recorded within 4 m and 20 m of the shark on 19% and 81% of interactions respectively, and paddleboats were within 4 m and 20 m of the shark on 34% and 80% of interactions respectively. Models outputs suggest that whale sharks display a higher probability of avoidance behaviour in the presence of motorized and paddle boats within 4 m of them. Similarly, the closer the motorized boats to the shark, the shorter the interaction duration. 6614: The Raja Ampat archipelago, protected by a network of nine MPAs since 2008 and a wellenforced shark and ray sanctuary since 2012, is known to host one of the largest manta ray populations in Indonesia. However, the population dynamics of reef manta rays in the region are still largely unknown. We used photo identification to count and track individual reef manta rays to better understand the local population dynamics in Raja Ampat. In order to provide critical information for management of this species in Raja Ampat’s MPAs, we used POPAN mark-recapture models to estimate reef manta population size and annual population growth rate. As of 31 December 2019, a total of 3,912 sightings were documented and 1,375 individuals identified from 45 sites across Raja Ampat over 16 years of observation. Females were more dominant than males at an observed sighting ratio of 3.15:2. Over 45% of these individuals were resighted at least once. The POPAN model restricted to 2009–2019 sighting data collected from the Dampier Strait and SE Misool MPAs (the two most regularly surveyed) estimated a superpopulation size of 1,467 individuals (821 females and 646 males). The most parsimonious model suggests that survival probability (phi) varied by sex, while sighting probability (p) differed between sex and year. Per capita birth/immigration rate (rho) was influenced by the delayed effects of the Multivariate ENSO Index (lagged MEI). Importantly, the model suggests an increase in the annual estimated population size of reef mantas in the Dampier Strait and SE Misool MPAs over the past decade. Our findings highlight the importance of Raja Ampat as a critical manta ray sanctuary and indicate a significantly positive impact of marine conservation measures in Raja Ampat on its large and thriving reef manta ray population, while also suggesting climate change impacts are to be expected.

6615: Anthropogenic inputs have caused atmospheric CO 2 levels to rise at an unprecedented rate and, unless curtailed, are anticipated to drastically increase the global surface and ocean temperatures. Due to warm-water input from local currents, Tasmania, Australia is a global hotspot for climate change and is one of the world’s fastest warming marine areas. In the southeast of the state, the Pittwater Estuary, part of a designated shark refuge area (SRA), is a key habitat that exhibits regular abiotic variations and is a primary pupping ground for the ‘conservation dependent’ school shark (Galeorhinus galeus). Temperature is one abiotic factor that can have a profound influence on the metabolism of ectothermic animals, with a 10˚C increase often translating to a doubling of metabolic rate. This research aims to understand how thermal variations may impact the physiology of neonatal school sharks. After capture and acclimation, animals were acutely (48h) exposed to environmentally relevant temperatures of 14°C, 18°C, and 22°C. Blood samples were collected every 24 hours during the trial and recovery, and routine metabolism was measured at key times throughout the experiment. Various blood parameters were analysed including haematocrit, haemoglobin, lactate and glucose content, and plasma osmolality. Oxygen consumption of the animals was measured in static respirometry chambers prior to experimentation, after 48 hours of acute exposure, and during recovery phase. Initial analysis shows that temperature has a significant effect on haematocrit, lactate, and glucose levels. Respirometry results are currently being analysed and further statistical tests will be applied to all data. Findings from this project will help to elucidate thermal tolerances of this species which may translate to determining habitat preferences, better modelling of population structures and environmental management, and an improved chance of recovery of the school shark population in the face of future global climate change.
6616: Conflict between humans and large predators is a longstanding challenge that can present negative consequences for humans and wildlife. Sharks have a global distribution and are considered to pose a potential threat to humans; concurrently many shark species are themselves threatened. Developing strategies for coexistence between humans and this keystone group is imperative. We assess blimp surveillance as a technique to simply and effectively reduce shark encounters at ocean beaches and determine the social acceptance of this technique as compared to an established mitigation strategy – shark meshing. We demonstrate the suitability of blimps for risk mitigation, with detection probabilities of shark analogues by professional lifeguards of 0.93 in ideal swimming conditions. Social surveys indicate strong social acceptance of blimps and preference for non-lethal shark mitigation. We show that continuous aerial surveillance can provide a measurable reduction in risk from sharks, improving beach safety and facilitating coexistence between people and wildlife.

6617: Unique individual markings are observed in numerous species, and have been used to understand their movement ecology and population dynamics. In terrestrial environments leopards have their spots, tigers their stripes and giraffes their pelage patterns, all unique to individuals and persistent through time. In East Africa, despite access to continuous habitat and the ability to move long distances, the pelage patterns of giraffes have diverged into different lineages, supported by genetic analyses, suggesting potential isolation due to pelage-based mate recognition. In the marine environment, numerous elasmobranch species display persistent individual markings through time, including grey nurse sharks Carcharinus taurus, whale sharks Rhincodon typus, and manta rays Mobula alfredi and M. birostris. Here we aimed to test whether the unique markings of manta rays can be used to infer relatedness between individuals within the same geographically separated sub-population, and whether these findings can provide insights into connectivity between sub-populations and potentially inform historic dispersal of the species. We collated 50 photographic identification (photo-ID) databases representing separate sub-populations of manta rays (M. alfredi n = 25 and M. birostris n = 25), totaling over 17,000 individuals. We used photo-ID in combination with machine learning and deep neural networks to analyse individual rays unique markings, and generate 256 embeddings relating to each individuals pattern. These were grouped at the sub-population level, to conduct investigations into relatedness within and between subpopulations. Preliminary results reveal significantly more variation in the markings between sub-populations of M. alfredi than within sub-populations (p < 0.0001). A PCA explained nearly 50% of the observed variance at the sub-population level. Our next step is to conduct similar analyses on M. birostris, where we predict we will see less variation explained by grouping at the sub-population level owing to the species movement ecology.
6618: Sawsharks are one of the least studied groups of sharks. In the last decade, however, we have learnt a lot about these creatures, especially in Australia. In this talk, I will present a summary of the research I have been involved in on these enigmatic sharks, including their ecology, their biology, and their stock status.
6619: As apex predators, sharks contribute to maintaining the balance of global marine ecosystems. Their populations are declining globally, yet many aspects of shark physiology and life history are poorly understood. Most of our understanding and management of sharks is based on our knowledge of their biology and interactions with other macro-organisms. Sharks live, however, in the ocean in a “soup” of microorganisms, and evidence from systems as diverse as plants, invertebrates and humans shows that microorganisms play critical roles in the health and function of macrobial hosts. We therefore need to understand how hostmicrobiome interactions function in sharks, so that we can develop robust conservation management tools. Here, we characterised the microbiome of Bull Sharks and Dusky Whalers in Sydney Harbour via 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. To understand what influences variation in microbial community structure within and between shark individuals and species, we quantified bacteria and archaea associated with multiple regions of the sharks’ bodies. We observed variation between body region, and between individuals and species. We discuss potential drivers of such variation and the microbial taxa and functions associated with these differences. This is the first step in understanding the role microorganisms play in shark health and function.

6620: Age and growth data are central to management or conservation strategies for any species. Circumstantial evidence suggests that male whale sharks grow to asymptotic sizes much smaller than those predicted by age and growth studies and consequently, there may be sexspecific size and growth patterns in the species. We tested this hypothesis by using stereovideo and photo-identification studies to estimate the growth rates of 54 whale sharks that were resighted over a period of up to a decade at Ningaloo Reef. We found that male growth patterns were consistent with an average asymptotic total length (TL) of approximately 8-9 m, a size similar to direct observations of size at maturity and much smaller than the sizes predicted by earlier modelling studies. Females were predicted to grow to an average asymptotic length of around 14.5 m. Males had growth coefficients of K = 0.088 yr-1, whereas limited resighting data suggested a growth coefficient of K = 0.035 yr-1 for females. Other data including re-sightings of an individual male over two decades, records of sex-specific maximum sizes of individuals captured in fisheries and data from juveniles growing in aquaria were also consistent with the suggestion of sex-specific growth profiles for the species. We argue that selection for sex-specific growth patterns could explain many of the otherwise enigmatic patterns in the ecology of this species including the tendency of the species to form aggregations of juvenile males in coastal waters.

6621: The energetics of an animal – its energy requirements and allocation to bodily processes – provides insight into trophodynamics and survival. Forecasting the plasticity of animal responses to environmental change can inform ecosystem and species management. Here we produce a bioenergetic model of the pelagic, longhorned pigmy devil ray Mobula eregoodoo, to estimate its relative energy allocation to various bodily processes, including reproduction. We also examined the use of energy reserves by mothers to investigate variability in reproductive strategies in elasmobranchs. We combined bioenergetic modelling and measurements of energy density to estimate relative energy costs for M. eregoodoo. We found M. eregoodoo uses up to 21.0% of their annual energy budget on growth and up to 2.5% on reproduction. Females appeared to use stored energy reserves during their reproduction. Their biennial reproductive cycle and use of energy stores aligns with general theory that ectotherms are capital breeders, and thus build energy reserves prior to reproduction. However, the use of energy reserves did not account for all of the costs of reproduction. This implies gravid females supplement reproductive costs with energy derived from their diet throughout gestation, as in an income breeding strategy. This suggests M. eregoodoo exhibits flexibility in fuelling reproduction depending on energy availability throughout the reproductive cycle, which may be prevalent in other elasmobranchs. Here we provide the first estimate of metabolic costs of gestation in an elasmobranch species and the first estimate of the relative cost of reproduction for any ray species. Energy costs and plasticity associated with highly variable reproductive strategies in elasmobranchs may influence long–term population viability under a rapidly changing environment.

6622: Three Southern Ocean skate species, B. eatonii, B. irrasa and B. murrayi, are commonly caught as by-catch in the Patagonian toothfish and mackerel icefish fisheries in waters surrounding Heard Island and McDonald Islands (HIMI) on the Kerguelen Plateau. However, no life history information exists for these species, which is necessary for the development of effective fisheries management strategies. Samples from 311 individuals (B. etonii-21, B. irrasa-269 and B. murrayi-21) were used to estimate age, growth and maturity parameters. This was accomplished by using vertebral ageing and a multi-model approach encompassing three growth models that were fitted to observed size-at-age data: (1) a von Bertalanffy growth model, (2) a Gompertz growth model, and (3) a logistic growth model. I will present preliminary results from this study that addresses the need for previously unknown biological information from these data-deficient species. Such information is important in understanding the risk of these species to harvest.

6623: There is currently a limited understanding of the morphological and functional organisation of the olfactory system in cartilaginous fishes, particularly when compared to bony fishes and terrestrial vertebrates. This study examines the ascending olfactory pathway of the brownbanded bamboo shark, Chiloscyllium punctatum, by assessing the relationship between several neuroanatomical indicators of olfactory abilities. Specifically, we 1) assess brain volumetrics (including olfactory bulbs, OBs) using an emergent X-ray computed tomography technique (diceCT), 2) estimate the convergence ratio of primary to secondary olfactory inputs as a proxy for olfactory sensitivity using transmission electron microscopy, and 3) provide a preliminary assessment of the different olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) types, relative abundance and distribution in the olfactory rosette using immunohistochemistry, histology and electron microscopy, and 4) correlate this with hydrodynamic modelling of incurrent water flow through the olfactory cavity. Together, the results indicate that relative OB volume remains a reliable proxy for assessing and comparing olfactory capabilities, there are three confirmed (out of a possible five) morphological ORN types identified, and there is some evidence of a lateral segregation of primary olfactory inputs within the OBs, suggesting a potential somatotopic organisation in this species. However, most ORNs are found to be ubiquitously distributed within the medial and lateral regions of the olfactory rosette, with only three sub-types found in significantly higher densities in medial lamellae. Hydrodynamic simulations in the olfactory cavities reveal that a differential distribution of ORN sub-types across the rosette may reflect adaptations in sampling specific water-borne chemicals and may guide subsequent tracking behaviour. This multimodal approach provides important quantitative data, which in turn, can inform the assessment of olfactory capabilities across a broader range of species in future.

6624: Movement of large marine predators can connect remote or isolated habitats, and create links that are key for maintaining connectivity within and between ecosystems. Given the extensive threats affecting coral reefs globally and the decline of top-order predators, a better understanding of their connectivity is critical is critical for understanding and mitigating the potential effects of their removal. We used a combination of acoustic telemetry data, network analysis, habitat modelling, and machine learning methods to quantify movement patterns and habitat use of three coral reef predators (grey reef shark Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos, silvertip shark Carcharhinus albimarginatus and red bass Lutjanus bohar). We also assessed and compared how movements and habitat preference influence connectivity within, and between two remote coral reef systems (Rowley Shoals and Scott Reef) off North-West Australia. Grey reef sharks displayed greater movement than silvertip sharks and red bass, with connectivity linking distant reefs and atolls. Movement patterns and connectivity was more extensive at Rowley Shoals than at Scott Reef. However, all three species preferred habitats with moderate to low structural complexity close to the reef and/or to passages in the reef crest, a pattern that was consistent between the two reef systems. Red bass movements resulted in local-scale connectivity between the lagoon and nearby forereef areas, whereas shark connectivity operated at broader scales creating greater linkages across distant areas within the reef systems. Despite some limitation in sample size we were able to compare movements of reef predators and identify species-specific habitat preferences driving habitat use and connectivity in two reef systems. Importantly, we show that existing spatial planning at these remote coral reefs is effective to protect local-scale movements of mesopredators, but that spatial protection at broader scales is still needed to effectively maintain the connectivity of large predators, which is crucial for the stability of isolated coral reef ecosystems.

6625: An understanding of the vertical movements of elasmobranchs across their range is crucial to defining critical habitat use and its overlap with anthropogenic activities, and subsequently managing such interactions. In this study, satellite telemetry was used to investigate the vertical habitat use of three oceanic manta rays Mobula birostris tagged on the northern coast of Peru. Vertical distributions skewed to surface waters (> 2m) were recorded by all three oceanic mantas, as well as patterns of reverse diel vertical migration, where vertical movements were significantly deeper at night. Data from two recovered tags sampling depth and temperature at 3- and 5-second frequencies revealed fine-scale behaviours, where individuals predominately remained in surface waters (> 2m) throughout the day, and oscillated up and down through a highly-stratified water column at night. Our results suggest that coastal vertical movements were motivated by a combined foraging and thermal recovery strategy, whereby oceanic mantas dived to the seabed to forage on demersal zooplankton at night and returned to surface waters to rewarm between dives, indicating that the coast of northern Peru may be a critical foraging habitat for oceanic mantas. High use of surface waters here, however, may put mantas at high risk to several anthropogenic impacts such as vessel strike, fishing gears, and unregulated tourism activities. Increased sample size and the use of other techniques, such as stable isotope analyses and animal-borne cameras, are required to validate our foraging and thermal recovery hypothesis and confirm this region as a foraging hotspot.

6626: Migratory marine megafauna undertake large scale (1000s km) movements to optimise foraging and breeding opportunities. Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) migrate seasonally between open ocean and nearshore locations, displaying vertical movements from the epipelagic to bathypelagic zones. Using oceanographic features such as water-mass transition zones, sea surface temperatures (SST) and bathymetry, coupled with vertical dive profiles, we examined the cues and drivers of vertical and horizontal movements displayed by this species during migration. A SPLASH tag was used to record find-scale vertical and horizontal movements of a whale shark travelling more than 5,000 km from Christmas Island to the Banda Sea from January – April 2008. After recovery of the tag, high resolution data archives were analysed to examine links between vertical movements, migration and oceanography. Depth profiles demonstrated distinct patterns suggestive of feeding, searching and transit behaviours that occurred within an optimal range of SST. Examination of surface times prior and post vertical movements provided evidence of behavioural thermoregulation. Additionally, SST influenced the trans-oceanic movements of this shark. Our results demonstrate the complexity of whale shark migration, highlighting the importance of oceanographic features to explain how and why marine megafauna migrate.

6627: Galapagos sharks, Carcharhinus galapagensis, are abundant in the Lord Howe Island Marine Park (LHIMP; covering State and Commonwealth waters) and are a key indicator species for monitoring and management. However, little is known about this species in the LHIMP and there is a pressing need to understand their movement ecology and behaviour because they regularly consume bait and hooked fish (depredation), leading to negative outcomes for fishers (social and economic) and sharks (injury or deliberate killing of sharks by fishers). We present data from an ongoing acoustic telemetry study of Galapagos sharks from January 2018 to January 2020, where 30 juvenile sharks were tagged with acoustic transmitters and charter fishing vessel activity was monitored using Vessel Monitoring System data. Sharks were detected throughout all months of the year, peaking in November, and they moved widely throughout the LHIMP, including crossing a deep-water (>1000 m) channel between the Lord Howe Island shelf and Ball’s Pyramid shelf. Kernel Utilisation Distribution analysis identified shark core use areas ranging from 1.2 - 217.6 km2 (mean ± SD = 50.7 ± 66.3 km2). Tag depth data indicated that sharks ranged from 0 - 95 m, with large variations in vertical movements between individuals. Generalised Additive Mixed Models revealed that shark occupancy at receiver locations (number of detections) was positively influenced by increasing fishing activity. Increasing bathymetric complexity and sea surface temperature also had a positive influence on number of detections. High residency values of up to 0.76 were recorded for three sharks at a location where fish waste is discarded, which may indicate a possible change in the movement patterns of these sharks due to the availability of this food source. This study provides detailed insights into the behaviour and movement ecology of this species and is a critical first step towards informing future research and community-driven management to reduce negative interactions between fishers and sharks in the LHIMP.

6628: Detections of tagged animals in passive acoustic telemetry arrays are primarily determined by the spatial configuration of the receivers. However, maintenance of multiple receivers is expensive, and there is a need to configure acoustic receiver arrays in a way that maximises detection probability while minimising cost. This study utilised data from a dense acoustic receiver array deployed off Port Stephens on the east coast of Australia at a known coastal aggregation site for white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) to assess how detection data of tagged white sharks in the area was affected by reducing the array size post hoc. Reduced arrays were sampled using three methods: fully random sampling as a base scenario, random sampling from spatially grouped clusters of receivers, and sampling of the top performing receivers. Using the top performing receivers, array size could be reduced by 60% (10 out of 25 receivers) and still reliably detect 100% of white sharks detected with the full array. Even with the random and clustered sampling methods this could be achieved with a 20% reduction in array size (20 out of 25 receivers). Reducing by 60% of the array size using the top performing receivers resulted in only an approximately 30% decrease in the average numbers of detections per visit of the tagged sharks (117 out of 171 detections), while reducing that same amount using the random and clustered sampling methods resulted in an approximately 60% decrease in average numbers of detections (68 and 71 out of 171 detections respectively). Although these results are specific to the Port Stephens array, the top receiver sampling method used in this study presents an experimental method of optimising placement of limited receiver resources that could be applied to design and assess spatial configurations of novel acoustic arrays for monitoring in similar habitats.

6629: Advances in biologging technology have enabled researchers to monitor the fine-scale movements and behaviour of numerous elasmobranchs, improving our understanding of how these animals behave and the biomechanics behind their swimming behaviours. With this said, there is very little information detailing the fine-scale behaviour of Batoids through the use of biologgers. In this study, we used high resolution multi-sensor biologging packages that record tri-axial acceleration, depth, temperature and speed to examine the fine-scale swimming behaviour and activity of the southern eagle ray (Myliobatis tenuicaudatus) in southeast Tasmania, Australia. A total of seven rays (874 ± 158 mm wing length; mean and ± SD) were tagged over two sampling periods: 4 individuals in 2014 and 3 individuals in 2020. Tag attachment time ranged from 68 h 43 m to 94 h 31 m (81 h 15 min ± 11 h 1 min; mean and ± SD) with a total of over 568 h of acceleration data recorded. Eagle rays exploited depths ranging from 0 - 38.18 m, swimming at an overall mean depth of 4.03 ± 4.17 m and experienced mean temperatures between 15.98 and 18.76 °C. All rays oscillated through the water column at relatively shallow angles, descending and ascending at an overall mean angle of -9.72 ± 4.76 ° and 9.32 ± 4.78° respectively. Initial investigations show that during descents, all animals exhibited periods of gliding behaviour. Further analysis will be undertaken to investigate this gliding behaviour to improve our understanding of why this behaviour is employed. Additional analyses will also investigate differences in diel behaviour and the biomechanics employed during swimming, providing the first insights into the fine-scale swimming behaviour and activity of the southern eagle ray and Batoids in general.

6630: The benefits of no-take MPAs, or marine reserves (MRs), for commercially exploited fish have been widely demonstrated, including in NZ, where reef-associated species have benefited from protection. In contrast, the effects of MRs on large and mobile species, such as sharks, are poorly studied in NZ. Given the current pressures facing shark populations, it is important to research the benefits that MRs may provide. Although most coastal MRs in NZ are relatively small, sharks may still benefit indirectly from the recovery of prey populations within protected habitats. This research thus aimed to investigate MRs in southern NZ to determine whether they have affected the distribution of coastal sharks. BRUVs (baited remote underwater video systems) were used to determine the relative abundance of sharks within six MRs and adjacent control sites in Fiordland and Stewart Island. 317 deployments were completed between April 2018 and December 2019. In addition, environmental DNA (eDNA) was integrated into the study during 30 deployments to compare the two techniques for detecting elasmobranchs, as well the efficacy of eDNA for MR monitoring. The main results showed that in Fiordland, mesopredatory sharks appear to be benefiting from protection, as a significant MR effect was observed. In contrast, a negligible MR effect was found for broadnose sevengill sharks. As broadnose sevengill sharks are a mobile top predator with a larger home range than mesopredators, these findings suggest that mesopredators with smaller home ranges are more likely to benefit from MRs in Fiordland. These results, therefore, emphasise the need to consider the size of MRs required for effective protection of species with different ranging behaviour. This study presents the first attempt to assess the effect of MRs on coastal elasmobranchs in NZ and will provide important insights into the applicability of eDNA as a tool for monitoring MRs.
6631: The life span of the Greenland shark is at least 272 years and may be as long as 500 years making this animal the longest living vertebrate on the planet. It was one of the lesser-known species of sharks up until 2016 when its extreme longevity was revealed. The finding that they live in the deep, dark Arctic waters for hundreds of years has captured the imagination of the world and the attention of scientists. How does an animal born in Shakespeare's time still patrol the deep today? This extreme longevity is particularly interesting with respect to the heart, because heart disease is synonymous with aging in humans. What structures do their hearts have that permit this extreme longevity? Does the heart underlie the ability of this shark to live so long? We investigated cardiac tissue from 8 sharks whose ages range between ~ 100±120 to 210 ±120 years old and found significant fibrosis, evidence of cardiomyocyte proliferation and regeneration and unusual mitochondrial biology. We did not find evidence of atherosclerosis. These findings will be discussed in relation to the idea of chronological age versus 'biological' age.

6632: Injection of neural tracers into selected branches of cranial nerves V, VII, IX and X that innervate respiratory muscles and the heart of the elasmobranch fish, Scyliorhinus canicula identified their progressive rostro-caudal distribution into discrete nuclei in the brainstem. Efferent activity recorded from nerves supplying respiratory muscles inserted on the jaws, hyomandibular and gill arches displayed sequential bursting activity, driving gill ventilation. This activity, which may be derive from a respiratory rhythm generator located in the reticular formation, was relayed via the trigeminal Vth nucleus, with subsequent activity in the VIIth, IXth and Xth nuclei reflecting their location in the brainstem. Forced ventilation is achieved by recruitment of feeding muscles, innervated by occipital and anterior spinal nerves. The heart and branchial (gill) circulation in elasmobranch fishes is innervated solely by the parasympathetic vagus nerve. Recordings from cardiac branches of the vagus showed two types of activity: units with regular, respiration-related activity and arrhythmic activity that increased during hypoxia and in response to J-recepter stimulation. Injection of neural tracers into the cardiac nerves revealed that cardiac, vagal, preganglionic neurons (CVPN) have their cell bodies in two locations in the brainstem: medial (m) within the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DVN) and a ventro-lateral scattered distribution (vl) outside of the DVN. Location of these cell bodies by insertion into the brainstem of recording micro-electrodes revealed that m cells showed respiration-related activity while vl cells did not. Both cell groups responded to mechanical stimulation of gill arches. Although tonic, peripheral electrical stimulation of cardiac branches of the vagus inhibited the heart, phasic stimulation recruited the heart at rates faster or slower than its intrinsic rate. A simple model attempting to explain the nature and significance of some of these interactions has been proposed.

6633: Despite their evolutionary success, many chondrichthyans are increasingly threatened with extinction as a result of human activities and the conservative life history traits of this group of fishes. In Mediterranean basin, the thornback ray (Raja clavata), represents among the Rajids the most commercially utilized species and it is actually included in the IUCN-RedList as Threatened species. In particular, in the West-Central Mediterranean basin, where the fishing activity is well-developed, R. clavata represents one of the most important by-catch species mostly for the bottom trawl and long line fishery. Despite being a very widespread species, some gaps still exist on its biology mostly on the growth pattern. The lack of biological data constitutes, for the Mediterranean, one of the impediments in order to assess and take appropriate management measures for this species. Indeed, stock-assessment models, particularly the analytical ones, require growth parameters as important input data. The aim of the present study is to fill this knowledge gap. Specimens of R. clavata were collected during the experimental trawl surveys, commercial landings and discard monitoring in Sardinia, Central-Southern Tyrrhenian, West Ionian and South Adriatic Sea. Thin sections of vertebrae were performed in order to determinate the age and calculate the von Bertalanffy growth function parameters for both sexes in each study area. Moreover, on specimens captured in Adriatic, Sardinia and West Ionian, the marginal increment analysis (MIA) of the vertebrae was also carried out as a semidirect ageing analysis validation. In the Adriatic, a mark-recapture experiment, marking by both external (spaghetti tags) and chemical (oxytetracycline injection) tags, 98 specimens of R. clavata was also realized. In total two recaptures after 11 and 14 months were recorded with an increment in total length respectively of 11.4 cm (from 49.5 to 60.9 cm) and 10.3 cm (from 63.5 to 73.8 cm). In both specimens recaptured the oxytetracycline mark together with the subsequent deposition of a completed annulus (one transparent and opaque ring) was observed on the sections of vertebrae.

6634: Morphometric characters have traditionally been used to describe fish population structures and differences between populations. They have been found to be of taxonomic importance in sex, race and species identification as well. Knowledge involving the taxonomy, systematics and life history of rays and skates that inhabit the Mediterranean basin is scarce. Up to date the importance of batoids in small-scale fisheries in the Greek waters is not well-known, possibly due to the taxonomic uncertainties concerning several taxa. The aim of this work was to present for the first time the morphometric characters of Raja clavata in the eastern Ionian Sea, in order to identify differences between sexes and compare them to other rajids in future references. Intraspecific variation in the external morphology of the thornback ray was investigated and described on the basis of 35 morphometric variables, from 77 females (140-780 mm in total length) and 63 males (135-690 mm in total length). For each morphometric value the mean, standard deviation, range and coefficient variation (CV) were estimated for each sex separately. Regression models were applied to estimate the relationships between each morphometric character and total length. The pattern of allometry for each parameter was established by testing the slope (b) of the obtained regression equations against isometry applying the Student's t-test. (b = 1 for length-length or 3 for length-weight). The length-weight relationship was determined according to the following equation: W=a*TLb. Differences between sexes were tested with t-test. 6635: The body (somatic) growth of individuals is a vital process that governs many aspects of a species' life history. Thus, knowledge about growth parameters is critical in many assessment methods. Such growth parameters are derived by relating individual length to age, with the latter commonly estimated from growth bands formed in calcified structures. Recent research, however, suggests that these structures cannot be used for aging in many elasmobranchs (sharks, rays and skates). Alternative methods from mark-recapture tagging data have been proposed in the past, but have not been rigorously tested on elasmobranchs. Therefore, the performance of seven different methods in estimating von Bertalanffy growth parameters for elasmobranchs is investigated here. The performance of the methods were evaluated in two ways: 1) Estimated growth parameters from simulated datasets that considered individual growth variability, measurement error and different scenarios for the length at capture, times at liberty and sample size were compared to the true growth parameters in the simulation; 2) Growth parameters were estimated from empirical mark-recapture tagging data for 15 different elasmobranch stocks and compared to literature growth parameters obtained from length-at-age information. Best practicies when only limited information from mark-recapture tagging data is available will be presented with practical applications and common pitfalls discussed.

6636: The different effects of fishing capture are not just immediate death; unwanted animals are released back into the environment to an unknown fate, as injuries and physiological, physical and behavioural consequences can ultimately lead to delayed mortality and/or impact their fitness. In teleosts, extensive research has highlighted that fisheries stress can negatively affect reproduction by impairing individuals' ability to contribute to the increase in population abundance and neonates' survival and performance. Despite being one of the most threatened aquatic taxa, data on the reproductive consequences of fishing capture for Chondrichthyans are virtually non-existent, jeopardizing the assessment of the real consequences of this practice and the development of effective fisheries management measures. We investigated whether trawling in semi-captive conditions impairs the reproductive success of pregnant Trygonorrhina dumerilii, a viviparous ray commonly caught as bycatch in southern Australian recreational and commercial fisheries. To do this we collected data on the occurrence of stillborn neonates, parturition timing, and neonates' dimension at birth, growth rate and performance (boldness, reflex, swimming and burying ability). Results highlighted that neonates born from mothers subjected to trawling simulation not only have a significantly lower body mass at birth, as recorded in a previous experiment, but also have a different allocation of yolk reserves and a lower growth rate, respond differently in the burying test, and swim for shorter distances when a predator attack is simulated. Smaller size and lower growth rate might expose neonates to a higher rate of predation, and similarly, the altered burying and swimming behaviour may be associated with a lower ability to escape from a predator. Further investigation is needed, but these first data suggest a possible reduction in neonates' survival rate and parents' fitness that can ultimately have severe repercussions on recruitment and population abundance in affected species.

6637: The fossil record of modern sharks mainly consists of isolated teeth due to their poorly mineralized cartilaginous endoskeleton and a continuous tooth replacement that forms thousands of teeth during a sharks' lifetime. As a result, phylogenetic analyses of extinct shark taxa are mostly based on isolated teeth and therefore often lead to ambiguous results. The great white shark Carcharodon carcharias is known since the late Miocene, a period in which a number of big lamniform sharks occurred, i.e., †Otodus megalodon, †Cosmopolitodus hastalis and †Carcharodon hubbelli, which vanished after the Plio-Pleistocene marine megafauna extinction (2.5 mya). The evolutionary history of the great white shark remains highly debated and two hypotheses have been proposed: (1) C. carcharias is closely related to the megatoothed sharks, including †O. megalodon; (2) C. carcharias shares a more recent common ancestor with mako sharks and descended from the broad toothed mako shark †C. hastalis. Although the latter hypothesis is currently favoured, the occurrence of a narrow- and a broad-toothed form of †C. hastalis further complicates the reconstruction of the evolutionary history of the great white shark. Here we report of an exceptional find of two well preserved shark skeletons of a juvenile (TL ~1.7m) and an adult (TL ~5m) †Cosmopolitodus hastalis from the late Miocene Pisco Formation of Peru, which display broad teeth. The presence of articulated jaws allowed us to reconstruct the tooth files of this species and thus a more accurate phylogenetic analysis of lamniform sharks based on dental characters could be performed, including extinct mako sharks, Isurus spp. Furthermore, geometric morphometric analyses are performed to visualize the morphospace occupation of Isurus, †Cosmopolitodus and Carcharodon. This combined approach allowed us to reconstruct the origin of Carcharodon carcharias and the dental transition from fossil mako sharks to the extant great white shark.

6638: Sharks are the marine top predators responsible for regulating population of other tertiary and quarternary consumers (i.e. fishes, seals and dolphins) and maintaining a naturally balanced trophic chain in the marine ecosystem. However, there is limited understanding on how these marine top predators are ecologically and biologically adapted to consume and digest such a wide variety of prey items, without hampering functional traits of the gastro-intestinal tract. Gastro-intestinal microbial community of sharks plays important different biological roles including development of vertebrae in juveniles, metabolising a wide variety of complex biomolecules, nutrient absorption and immune system response. Hammerhead sharks are characterised by intraspecific ontogenetic and sex partitioning of resources (i.e. habitat and diet) as reflected by satellite tagging, genetics and stable isotope analyses. However, it's unknown how gut microbial biota changes between juvenile and adult sharks (ontogenetic partitioning of resources) and also between female and male individuals (sex partitioning of resources) within species. This study analysed gut microbial community structure and composition of two Sphyrna spp. based on 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing at both intraspecific and interspecific levels. DNA was extracted using Zymobiomics DNA miniprep kit and sequences generated using paired-end sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform following the manufacturer's instructions. Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology (QIIME) analyses revealed non-significant changes in microbial community structure between juvenile and adult individuals and also between sexes within each species. The core microbiota included Actinobacteria, Flavobacteria, Protobacteria and Firmicutes whereas Proteobacteria were the most abundant phylum. This suggests gut microbiome of hammerhead sharks may be shaped by broader biological factors such as the host genotype and ambient environmental conditions rather than diet.

6639: This study contributes to the abundance - biomass index, length-weight relationship (LWR) and bathymetric distribution of four deepwater elasmobranches (sharks) species obtained by the trawl fishing in the Antalya Bay (Eastern Mediterranean). For bathymetric distribution and survey, a total of 15 successful hauls were done with an approximately 800 km2 swept area, in five bathymetric strata within 100 m interval between the depths of 200 - 700 m. As yet, a total of 25 specimens of C. granulosus, 586 specimens of E. spinax, 613 specimens of G. melastomus and 99 specimens of S. blainvillei were caught between the depths of 200-700 m. Linear regressions were significant for all species (p < 0.05), with r2 values are greater than 0.950 as a whole. 6640: Our oceans are facing tremendous human-induced changes, including warming. As the temperature has increased, sudden warming events designated as marine heatwaves have become longer and more frequent with significant implications over marine ecosystems. As a crucial element of the marine environment, sharks may also be affected by these environmental changes. Exposure to ocean warming has shown to impact shark's predatory behavior, metabolism and overall fitness. However, the effects that a marine heatwave may have on these animals' physiology has not been addressed previously. Thus, the focus of our study was to investigate the impact of a marine heatwave (Δ3 °C) on the heamatological and respiratory systems of a juvenile temperate shark (Scyliorhinus canicula). To address this question, sharks were exposed to two treatments: control (18 °C) and category II marine heatwave (21 °C) for 15 days. We then analyzed the i) normal blood cell counts (e.g. erythrocytes, leucocytes and thrombocytes), ii) type and amount of EMNAs (erythrocyte nuclear morphological abnormalities), iii) spleen and heart to body ratios and iv) ventilation rates (before, initially and during the heatwave). According to our study, exposure to a category II marine heatwave drastically changed normal blood cell counts and ventilation rates. More specifically, the number of erythrocyte cells decreased, while the number of leukocyte and thrombocyte cells increased. Moreover, the amount of ventilation also increased. These findings may evidence that, during a sudden warming event, shark's ability to transport oxygen in red blood cells, linked to their need to ventilate more, might be significantly impaired. Furthermore, an increase of leukocytes and thrombocytes may explain the vulnerability and stress related to the increased temperature. As marine heatwaves are expected to aggravate with anthropogenic climate change, there is an urgency that should eager us to manage and mitigate its impacts.

6641: Monitoring trends in shark body size and weight is fundamental for understanding their life history traits and elucidating population dynamics. Traditionally, size and weight information is acquired through invasive techniques, involving capture and handling. These protocols may undermine conservation efforts by causing physical damage, behavioral alterations, premature birth and even the death of the captured animals. This study tested the effectiveness of laser photogrammetry as a non-invasive technique for measuring morphometrics from five shark species housed in aquariums. The measured morphometrics were examined in regression analyses to provide a comprehensive set of lineal relationships for the estimation of shark total length and weight. The results obtained indicate that (1) this approach is effort and cost-effective; (2) laser metrics are highly precise, which ensures the reliability of the gathered morphometric information; and (3) accurate total length and weight estimates can be obtained from short morphometrics. These insights indicate that laser photogrammetry is a useful technique for assessing growth and life history parameters from free-swimming sharks. Therefore, this technique may constitute a valuable tool for aquariums to monitor sharks' health status and determine food requirements and medication doses. Furthermore, it has the potential to provide useful insights when applied to monitor sharks in their natural environments in order to implement effective management strategies. The compiled also models ease the obtention of total length and weight data, providing a long-needed resource in shark monitoring programs.

6642: Sharks play both essential and diverse functional roles in marine ecosystems, having a remarkably long and successful evolutionary history. However, overfishing and habitat degradation, amidst other challenges, have ensued a steep population decline over the past decades. As CO2 emissions continue to increase, ocean acidification (OA) may come to pose an additional challenge to this group. In the present study, we investigated the potential impacts of OA-conditions (pCO2 ~900 µatm | Δ -0.3 pH units) over the embryonic development and juvenile metabolic physiology of a temperate shark, Scyliorhinus canicula. Aiming to evaluate the consequences of early exposure to high CO2 conditions, newly laid eggs were reared in either control or OA-treatment and, once hatched, individuals incubated under high CO2 were redistributed between both treatments. Both embryonic development, namely embryogenesis duration, hatching success, embryo activity, growth rate, body ratios, and juvenile metabolism, specifically their food intake, routine metabolic rate, maximum metabolic rate and aerobic scope, were evaluated. Overall, there were no significant changes in neither their development nor their metabolic physiology, regardless of early exposure to high CO2 levels. While this study highlights the coping capacity of sharks towards ocean acidification, the multiple and unpreceded pressures placed upon this group have the potential to undermine their inherent resilience. Hence, further research regarding different aspects of their biology and the numerous threats of the near-future is necessary to fully understand how this group may fare in the oceans of tomorrow.

6643: Serum biochemistry and hematology profile are used to assess the physiological status of animal individuals and populations. Therefore, establishing reference intervals for serum biochemical and hematological analytes for wild populations of marine keystone species is important for their conservation. However, no such intervals have been established to date for many species in the Eastern Mediterranean, including the dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) and sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus). In the Mediterranean, C. obscurus and C. plumbeus are classed as data deficient and endangered species, respectively, according to the IUCN Red List. This study aims to establish reference intervals for serum biochemical and hematological analytes in these two species. Blood samples have been collected from wild dusky and sandbar sharks captured during the tagging seasons that Morris Kahn Marine Research Station has been conducting since 2016. In the winters of 2016 and 2017, blood samples were obtained from 14 C. obscurus and 7 C. plumbeus individuals. This ongoing study has and will further expand this database during the winters of 2018 and 2019. To this point, serum samples of 19 C. obscurus (18 females and one male) and 12 C. plumbeus (all males) individuals were analyzed by spectrophotometry using an autoanalyzer, including 15 analytes: urea, total proteins, total bilirubin, glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides, inorganic phosphorus, chloride, sodium, potassium, total calcium, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), amylase, and creatine kinase (CK). For nine animals (four C. obscurus and five C. plumbeus), packed cell volume has been measured by centrifugation of heparinized capillaries, and manual leukocyte counts on blood smears have been done by microscopy. Preliminary results of serum biochemistry of both species are mostly consistent with findings of previous studies describing C. plumbeus in the Western Atlantic and other shark species in different locations. However, several analytes showed different values than previously described.

6644: Chondrichthyes (sharks, rays and chimaeras) are the most basal jawed vertebrate lineage possessing the basic features of the human innate and adaptive immune systems, and thus are a key taxon to understand the emergence and evolution of vertebrate adaptive immunity. However, the few studies conducted to date have not provided a clear picture of the complexity of the genes involved in adaptive immunity in this oldest extant vertebrate class. Our results show that for the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I genes, involved in antigen presentation to T cells and Nature Killer (NK) cells, there is indeed a very high diversity in genetic lineages and copy number variation across taxa, at least as complex as has been found in mammals. A new lineage of MHC-linked class I genes was found in all chondrichthyans, which appears to be single copy and likely monomorphic in Elasmobranchs but multicopy in Holocephalans. The predicted peptide-binding region is perfectly conserved in all Elasmobranchs tested, suggesting that the resulting protein(s) bind a unique set of peptides in all sharks and rays, rather than to allele-specific sets of peptides typical of the polymorphic classical class I molecules. Two previously reported yet poorly studied lineages of nonclassical MHC class I genes in cartilaginous fish were also examined but have only been found in sharks so far, although this may be due to a paucity of data for batoids and holocephalans. Our data clearly demonstrate that there was a division of labor among MHC class I lineages early in vertebrate evolution, with each lineage likely presenting different types of antigens to different subsets of T cells and/or NK cells.

6645: Elasmobranchs are among the marine species more threatened even by a moderate fishing intensity. Consequently, many elasmobranch species are now included in the red list of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Effective management of endangered shark species requires a good understanding of their life histories traits. In this study, we estimated some growth and maturity parameters of two vulnerable shark species Mustelus mustelus (Linnaeus, 1758) and M. punctulatus (Risso, 1827) in the central Mediterranean Sea. The study is based on the analyses of vertebral growth bands; three different asymptotic growth models (e.g. VBGF, Logistic and Gompertz) have been applied with back-calculated length-at age data obtained using the Fraser-Lee equation. Results highlight that M. mustelus is a longer living species than M. punctulatus reaching also bigger sizes-at-ages. The growth parameters (sexes combined) of the two species were: L∞: 185 cm, K/year: 0.16 and t0: -3.2 (M. mustelus); and L∞: 105.5 cm and K/year: 0.27 with a t0:-1.4 (M. punctulatus). The growth curve of M. mustelus indicates an absolute annual growth rate of 15 cm by year during the first five years of life (i.e. between 35 and 105 cm TL). 6646: The Norwegian skate Dipturus nidarosiensis (Storm, 1881) has only recently been recorded in the western and central Mediterranean Sea along the coast of Sardinia, off Algeria in Alboran Sea, in southern Adriatic and western Ionian Sea. An ancient presence of the Norwegian skate was hypothesised, despite its misclassification between D. nidarosiensis and other species from the same genus Dipturus. Infact its misclassification in the fishery data, mostly among the following species: D. oxyrinchus, D. batis, D. nidarosiensis and Rostroraja alba has not been uncommon since ancient times. These errors could have led to the underestimation of the risk of a dramatic decline and collapse of the spawning stock. Morevover, in the IUCN Red-List, the Norwegian skate is listed as near-threatened and it is considered rare in both the northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean areas. Furthermore, due to its biological characteristics, which are similar to other elasmobranchs, such as low fecundity, slow growth and high length at first maturity, it is particularly vulnerable to environmental and anthropogenic pressures. From 2005 to 2019, the catches of Norwegian skate specimens were mostly repeated in two areas: the Sardinian Seas and Adriatic-Ionian area. In these two areas, a total of 64 specimens were caught and 10 morphological measurements and 6 meristic counts were taken on all captured specimens. The present study describes and characterizes, from a morphological point of view, the Norwegian skate specimens caught in the Sardinia Seas (Central Mediterranean Basin) and southern Adriatic-Ionian Sea (Central Mediterranean Basin). Morphological comparisons are made to provide further morphological keys for a correct classification of this species in the Mediterranean Basin. A multivariate approach analysis highlighted that some morphological features could be used to recognize two separated groups for the sampling areas (Sardinia; Adriatic-Ionian area), sex (male; female) and ontogenetic development (juveniles, adult).

6647: The Rajidae is a highly diverse family of elasmobranch fishes, including more than 285 species. Raja clavata is the most common and widespread skate in the N.E. Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, and one of the dominant species in commercial landings. Currently, available data are either incomplete or incorrect due to the high level of morphological variability in rajids. Diversity of coloration patterns or polychromatism, has been reported previously for batoids (rajids, daysatids, potamotrygonids), which causes misidentification among closely related species. Therefore, morphological features are not always indicative of species relatedness. Additionally, several diagnostic characters distinctively visible in adults can be less evident in juveniles, making the taxonomy of younger specimens more difficult. In an attempt to minimize the gaps in our current knowledge on batoid biological traits, taxonomic issues were brought up in the Rajidae family. Specifically, taxonomic confusion had to be resolved among R. clavata, Raja polystigma and Raja montagui, which were caught in the eastern Ionian Sea. Our aim was to present an atlas of the polychromatism patterns of R.clavata, following the reliable identification of specimens using DNA sequencing. We applied DNA barcoding on 33 samples with taxonomic difficulties, and used the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (COI). We demonstrated that all 33 specimens were identified as R. clavata, confirming that the species exhibits high levels of polychromatism in the Ionian Sea like in Tunisia, Algeria and Marocco. Our findings show that accurate data from scientific surveys and landings are essential to assess conservation status and to develop suitable protection and management plans.

6648: In the past few years the knowledge on diseases and the disorders of elasmobranchs housed in public aquariums has increased, with particular reference to spinal deformities, thyroid pathologies, neoplasms, reproductive disorders and transmissible diseases (viral, bacterial mycotic and parasitic). Among these, bacterial infections mainly due to Vibrionaceae play an important role as often related to episodes of mortality in the presence of predisposing conditions. Vibrio harveyi (syn. V. carchariae) has been often associated with phenomena of meningitis or skin ulcers in different species of sharks. In the Aquarium of Cattolica (RN) over 100 elasmobranchs belonging to 16 different species are present. In the last few years, most of the occurred episodes of mortality in sharks were caused to bacteria, in particular V. harveyi. In detail, this pathogen has been identified as aetiological agent of disease outbreaks leading to the death of 4 young bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo), 5 (4 juvenile and one adult) of black tip shark (Carcharhinus melanopterus), 3 juvenile bamboo shark (Chiloscyllium punctatum) and one adult nurse shark (Ginglymostoma cirratum). In these 2 last species also V. fischeri and Photobacterium damselae subsp. damselae were respectively isolated. In all cases meningitis and enteritis were observed. All episodes of mortality occurred during the quarantine period or after their transfer to a new tank. Therefore, opportunistic pathogens such as V. harveyi need to be considered relevant for the health of fish maintained in aquarium ecosystem and the application of effective management protocols can be useful to reduce the stress conditions to which the animals can be subjected especially during the phases following their transport and acclimatization to new habitat.

6649: Elasmobranchs are among the most threatened vertebrates on the planet, especially due to overfishing and habitat destruction. Despite this level of threat, the use of techniques to control their reproduction has been scarcely investigated as an approach to protect them in the wild or in captivity. Our main objective was to apply techniques commonly used in other fish species to achieve reproductive control in elasmobranchs. Four model species (Scyliorhinus canicula, Scyliorhinus stellaris, Galeus melastomus and Raja montagui) were the target with which to develop techniques that can be extrapolated to other species. Target species were obtained from fishing by-catch and from public aquaria. Urogenital and reproductive systems were anatomically described, and hepatosomatic and gonadosomatic indexes were calculated from by-catched species. Oocyte diameter was measured every month to establish their reproductive status through the year. Both in vivo and post-mortem extraction of sperm was achieved, by massage and gentle pressure near the urogenital pores or by catheterization with a urethral catheter. Spermatozoa were motile after activation with a Ringer solution adapted to elasmobranchs even when extracted from the seminal vesicle of dead fish stored at 4°C for 48 h. Sperm obtained from the cranial portion of the epididymis seemed to be immature and remained immotile in the 4 species, while it could be activated when was obtained from the caudal portion of the epididymis. Sperm volume and spermatozoa characteristics, such as size and number of helical gyres of the sperm head, size of midpiece and flagellum, and complexity and type of spermatozoa aggregates, were determined. Despite obvious sperm motility, large cell size (total length: 116-198 µm) made impossible its evaluation by standard CASA protocols. The techniques developed with our 4 target species were also tested in other specimens including a nurse shark (Gynglymosotoma cirratum) and a lesser devil ray (Mobula hypostoma).
