6650: Sharks of the order Lamniformes comprise seven families with 15 extant species, including some of the most iconic shark species, like the great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) and †Otodus megalodon. Lamniform sharks have a rich fossil record dating back to the Cretaceous with the oldest confirmed members of this group being known from the Barremian (125-130 mya). However, the origin of this group remains ambiguous, since sharks of the genus †Palaeocarcharias, small benthic sharks superficially resembling carpet sharks (Orectolobiformes) that are known from Middle Jurassic deposits (170 mya), are discussed to belong to this order. We used high resolution micro-CT scans obtained with the micro-CT scanner SkyScan 1173, to examine the tooth mineralization patterns of extant and fossil shark taxa and found three different tooth histologies: (1) orthodont teeth that have hollow pulp cavities surrounded by orthodentine, (2) osteodont teeth that have osteodentine and lack of orthodentine, (3) and pseudoosteodont teeth that have an osteodont core, which is surrounded by orthodentine. Our results show that exclusively osteodont teeth are only present in lamniform sharks and, therefore, suggest that this character represents a synapomorphic trait for this group. Additionally we could show that †Palaeocarcharias stromeri shares this unique tooth histology pattern with all lamniform sharks, suggesting that this shark indeed is the oldest known ancestor of this group.

6651: Data accumulated during a taxonomic study of Haematozoa of Rajidae (Elasmobranchs) have allowed a bioecological approach to the parasitism of the two most frequent, Trypanosoma rajae Laveran and Mesnil, 1902 and Haemogregarina sp Danilewsky, 1885 whose respective prevalences are: 15.06% and 9.58%. 8.2% of associations of the two parasites have been observed. The study was conducted on 113 rays belonging to four species of Rajidae (Raja asterias Delaroche, 1809 Raja miraletus Delaroche, 1809; Raja radula Linnaeus, 1758 and Raja undulata Lacepede, 1802) caught at two sampling sites on the Algiers coast: the port of Cap Djinet and the port of Bou Haroun. Statistical analysis of the data revealed a link between the age of the hosts and the parasitism. In the case of Trypanosoma rajae infestation, the oldest rays are the most infested, while in the case of infestation by Haemogregarina sp. host parasitism evolves in the same direction as age until a certain stage beyond which individuals defaunent of their parasites. An impact of parasitism on the health of the hosts was sought by the comparison of formulas leukocytes of parasitized and uninfected specimens; within the limits of the sample examined. The results do not allow any conclusion on any impact on the leucocyte composition of the infested hosts. The general parasitism observed in Cape Djinet (40.14%) seems more important than that of Bou Haroun (30.77%); the numbers treated, do not allow to conclude to a significant difference statistically.

6652: The spotted dogfish Scyliorhinus canicula is the common and widely distributed elasmobranch in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Recent studies have shown that this species has an important role in the trophic scheme of demersal fish communities, representing an important trophic link between invertebrates and larger predatory fish. It is also appreciated for the quality of its meat; this increases its commercial interest. Several studies suggest that this species is particularly susceptible to changes in environmental conditions, including temperature and oxygen availability, as well as exposure to pollutants. This can induce oxidative stress that in turn can lead to cellular damage and detrimental effects. Taking this into consideration, the evaluation of oxidative stress biomarkers assumes special importance, in an ecological, economical and public health perspective. However, to date no reference intervals for several oxidative biomarkers, have been reported for this shark. The aim of this study is to establish specific reference values for oxidative biomarkers in target tissues of S. canicula in order to assess the physiological status of the animal. Tissues samples (heart, muscle, gills, liver) have been collected from 32 spotted dogfish captured in the Mediterranean Sea (Follonica) during the period February-May 2018. Tissues were homogenized and subjected to spectrophotometric assays to asses the activity of SOD and LDH enzymes, markers of antioxidant activity and aerobic-anaeribic metabolism, as well as the levels of protein carbonylation and lipid peroxidation, indicative for oxidative stress damage. Preliminary results has been also analyzed in relation to tissue heavy metal accumulation.

6653: Atmospheric carbon dioxide has been increasing since the industrial revolution with a concomitant decrease in ocean pH, a phenomenon designated as ocean acidification (OA). OA may pose a threat to fundamental marine organisms, such as sharks. In this context, the current experiment aimed to test the effects of OA on different hematological parameters of the juvenile small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula). Eggs were collected and randomly placed in either Control (pCO2 ~ 400 µatm) or High CO2 (pCO2 ~ 900 µatm, Δ -0.3 pH units) treatments, throughout the entire embryogenesis plus ~90 days after hatching. Hematological analysis was conducted on the number of normal blood cells (erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes); presence of erythrocytes with nuclear abnormalities, and the erythrocyte cytoplasm to nucleus ratio was measured. Spleen and heart to body ratios were also evaluated. Overall, OA did not elicit significant differences in the studied parameters. Nonetheless, the decreasing trend in thrombocyte counts, which may have implications over clotting time, should foster further research. Although the present findings indicate that these sharks are possibly resilient to the prolonged OA exposure, future studies should scrutinize the scarcely recognized multi-stressors impacts (i.e. marine heatwaves, hypoxia, pollution, etc.) that sharks potentially will have to endure in the near future.

6654: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) is the world's longest-lived vertebrate, with an estimated lifespan of 392±120 years. However, the mechanisms facilitating their extreme longevity remain unknown. Here, we generate the first de-novo transcriptome for the Greenland shark, as a tool to investigate the basic biology and ageing of elasmobranchs. Cardiac tissue from six Greenland sharks, between the approximate ages of 110 and 219 years, was collected from Bredefjord and Qaqortoq Fjords, Greenland, in the spring of 2017. A total of 236 million read pairs survived quality control, and were used to produce the transcriptome. The assembly process generated 149,000 transcripts with an N50 of 1,202bp, and a BUSCO score of 76.2%, making the transcriptome comparable in quality to that of other published squaliform elasmobranch transcriptomes. BLAST searching the transcripts against the whale shark (Rhincodon typus) genome identified 7,218 genes. Gene enrichment analysis revealed a significant over-representation of genes linked to mitochondrial function and ribonucleoprotein biogenesis, which is particularly interesting given that changes in mitochondrial quality are associated with many age-related diseases. A rank regression against total length, a proxy for age, identified 205 genes (205/7,218; 5x10-2 > p > 1x10-3, 0.99 > |r| > 0.88) displaying a significant correlation with length, including genes associated with antioxidant pathways, cardiomyocyte regeneration, and a dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype. This dataset is a valuable resource for future studies on the Greenland shark, particularly when investigating the molecular mechanisms underpinning age-related changes in the shark's physiology.

6656: Researches using stable isotopes analysis (SIA) of carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) in blood components (red blood cells and plasma) are still lacking, considering the challenge of sample collection in remote areas. There is poor information regarding the effect of tissue biochemical composition on isotopic ratios and there are few comparisons among different taxa in this regard. We explore the possibility that tissues biochemistry of different taxa affect isotopic results. During 2016 and 2017 we collected blood samples from shortfin mako sharks (Isurus oxyrinchus, n=70) and Guadalupe fur seals (Arctocephalus philippii townsendi, n=25). All the samples were centrifuged to obtain plasma in the case of mako sharks and serum for fur seals and then prepared for SIA. We did not find significant differences in δ15N values between the two species, but we found significant differences comparing δ13C in plasma of mako sharks (δ13C= -17.6 ± 0.9 ‰) and in serum of fur seals (δ13C= -20.3 ± 1.2‰). Furthermore, we tested the possible effect of different anticoagulants for sharks and lipids effect for Guadalupe fur seal samples. We did not find differences between species in both tests. The lack of significant differences in δ15N between the Guadalupe fur seal and the shortfin mako shark is likely related to their similar trophic level. The δ13C differences between the two species are probably due to serum and plasma biochemical characteristics, like lipid percentage in each species, more than differences in foraging area. These biochemistry characteristics in tissues are related to different adaptations in each taxon. This study shows the importance of developing more research on the influence of biochemistry features on isotopic results, because that blood component biochemistry may play a more important role in influencing isotopic signature than differences in foraging area.

6657: Skates (Rajidae) are oviparous Chondrichthyes which lay egg-cases on the sea floor, and while data of egg-cases' occurrence along the strandline exist, underwater field data helping to determine spawning grounds (presence of viable egg-cases) are very limited. During a demersal survey in Namibian waters in 2019, large quantities (5 to 21 kg) of ray egg cases were found at three locations. The egg cases were identified as belonging to the genus Rajella, possibly of the species Rajella barnardi or R. leopardus. These species were present together with the cases; confirmed by the trawl catch species identification. Two of the stations were located off the continental slope of Cape Cross not apart from each other, while the third one was located north off Cape Frio. The area can be described as confluence zone where warm tropical waters coming from the north meet subtropical colder waters flowing form the south creating a counter-clockwise water mass movement. The sites were at depths between 520 and 618 m. Over 90% of the cases were empty, the rest contained a yolk, which seemed to have been fertilized. Because the cases are made of collagen which breaks down very slowly, it is difficult to know when the older cases have been laid, but the empty ones were easily differentiable from the new-laid both by the texture and color. Although the species are not uncommon in these waters, the collection of such amounts of egg cases, both old and new, is an unusual observation pointing to a potential spawning area. This knowledge will help drawing a more detailed picture on the biology and distribution of the local species, which will contribute to improving their management.

6658: Over the past 30 years we have pioneered the use of archival and satellite tags to study the ecology, physiology and habitats of highly migratory tunas and lamnid sharks. Our research has provided large data sets on many species of endothermic fishes and sharks including the salmon, white and mako sharks, bluefin, and yellowfin tunas and billfishes. The value of having acquired these large data sets has given us a better understanding of their migrations, ecology, physiology, and behaviors of these animals in the wild. Combining these electronic tag data with fisheries data and genomics are key approaches for establishing life history, population biology, and protections for highly mobile predators in the open sea.

6659: In Israel, dusky and sandbar sharks (genus Carcharhinus) aggregate every winter at the warm water discharge of coastal power plants. This over wintering pattern is likely thermoregulatory in nature. Sightings of these species are increasingly rare in the Mediterranean, where shark populations have declined by 95% over the last decades. Sharks were tracked by acoustic telemetry, which enables detecting acoustic transmitters ('tags') by fixed underwater receivers. Since 2015, 17 sharks have been caught, measured and tagged in Hadera's hot waters, using acoustic tags and satellite tags. Acoustic tags are inserted into the shark's abdominal cavity, and satellite tags were attached to the dorsal fins. Both acoustic and satellite transmitters also recorded depth, and water temperature. Sharks were detected at the site for a long period (66 days ± 33.3 SD), and remained in the hot discharge while sea temperature kept decreasing. Daily movement analysis show sandbar sharks remain close to the bottom during daytime and moved to shallower water at night, while dusky sharks occupied very shallow water at all times. Data retrieved from one satellite tag showed a sandbar shark maintained the daily depth movement throughout its journey in open water. Temperature analysis show sharks stay within the elevated temperature zone throughout the season, away from the ambient temperature, until they leave the area completely. While one theory maintains that these aggregations are related to the gestation period in females, the residency of both female and male sharks suggest both genders benefit from the warm water. It is possible, that sharks are changing migration to warmer areas with the warm water at the station. Large scale movement study is crucial to understand the migration routes of these species in the Mediterranean Sea, and the implications of this phenomenon on their movement.

6660: The sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus is one of the biggest sharks inhabiting the Mediterranean. It is a cosmopolitan species and wellknown from Boncuk Cove in Mediterranean coast of Turkey. Primary nursery grounds, defined as areas where parturition occurs, of Boncuk Cove C. plumbeus population. The aim of study is to determine secondary reproduction and nursery area of sandbar shark from Yumurtalık Bight, Eastern Mediterranean Sea. On 24-27 July 2017, Sandbar shark specimens were accidentally caught at a depth of 7 to 9 m off the Yumurtalik Bight (36°44'44.39"N, 35°42'22.77"E) by a pelagic bluefish longline. A total of 8 specimens (4 females and 4 males) were transported to the laboratory on ice. Each fish was measured for total length to the nearest 0.1 cm, weight (W) was weighted to the nearest 0.1 g and sex was determined by the presence of claspers. Total lengths and weights of C. plumbeus specimens were 54.5-61.0 cm, 930 - 1484 g, for males and 49.6 - 62.4 cm, 918 - 1568 g, respectively for females. In shark species, the embryo is connected to the mother by an umbilical cord. The umbilical scars are still clearly visible on these newly born sharks. 6661: This study aims to provide general information regarding the effect of environmental factors on the occurrence of white sharks during ecotourism in Guadalupe Island, Mexico. The white sharks presence and environmental conditions were registered each hour during August-November of 2012-2014 in Rada Norte Bay (RNB). Analyzed environmental factors included sea surface temperature (SST), wind direction and speed, tide, moon phase, cloud cover, and water visibility. Sighting records were used to describe the white shark's probability of occurrence in relation to environmental factors, geographical position, and hour. Generalized additive models were applied using the presence/absence of the sharks as response variable according to the following categories: 1) Immature males; 2) Mature males; 3) Immature females; 4) Mature females. A total of 6,266 sightings of white sharks was registered according to sexual maturity during 98 days at RNB. Median from these records was 59 sightings per day (S.E.=5.96), and 9.82 sightings per hour (S.E.=1.22), with no significant differences in the sightings per hour related to the year (H2,90=6.35; P = 0.04), as confirmed by Bonferroni test. Regarding the month, a higher number of sightings per hour were observed during August (H3,90=21.20; P < 0.01), with no significant differences between the following months. The model for mature males suggests that there is a higher occurrence in the south part of RNB when SST is lower than 21°C, after new moon, and at any hour. In contrast, immature males' occurrence was higher in the west, during warm SST > 22°C, after full moon nights, and in the morning hours. Regarding females, mature individuals showed a higher probability of occurrence in the east, during warm SST > 23° C, early morning, and the last hours of the day. Explanations for these results will be discussed toward a potential segregation of white sharks in Guadalupe Island.

6662: Spatiotemporal variation of the deposition of skate's eggcases on beaches of the french metropolitan coast from 2005 to 2017 was studied. Due to the lack of knowledge on skates nowadays, we hypothesized that eggcases' distribution can provide additional informations for fishery surveys and spatio-temporal variations. Data were provided by a citizen science program involving 1900 volunteers. The proximal goal of this project was to evaluate the influence of environmental factors, detect a long term evolution and define massive strand areas. A methodological challenge consisted in performing a reliable analysis on a large dataset (~465000 eggcases, 1077sites) based on opportunistic data where absence or sampling effort were not notified. Fortunately, we were able to mobilize a second dataset (~240000 eggcases, 30sites) which is more standardized allowing to investigate temporal autocorrelation. Furthermore for spatial analysis, we established a 5 km buffer from the coast to collect all types of habitat around. Eggcases of seven species were encountered, mostly Raja undulata, R.clavata and R.brachyura. Adequate analysis performed on the two dataset provided the same results within and between year variations. The evolution of egg's deposition within a year shows a neat phenology with a peak of increase during winter followed by a decrease during summer. Eggcase's deposition from undulate rays tend to increase significantly (26%) throughout the years. However, for other species it didn't show any inter-annuals significant trends. Undulate's eggs were mostly found near littoral rocks and coarse sands and tend not to be present near deep habitats while thornback's eggs can be found near both deep and tidal zones. They are qualified as opportunistic for habitats and depth according to literature and experts. Blonde ray's eggs were found near shallow zones in rocks and sandy bottoms. These results suggest that egg's deposition of skates over time can allow us to have more information on the biology and ecology of species.

6663: Active acoustic surveys have been increasingly utilized as a non-extractive method for abundance estimation. These rely on species identification based on the focal animal's morphology, i.e., the dimensions of gas-filled structures such as the swim bladder, lungs, or other air cavities. Acoustic studies on elasmobranchs, which do not possess such structures, have dealt with the reflectivity of particularly large species or were unable to produce reliable size estimates, a prerequisite for density indexing. Furthermore, acoustic surveys typically employ narrow beam sonars which, with respect to highly-scattered populations, are mainly useful where animals are already known to occur as opposed to open-ocean waters. Thus, despite the potential usability of this method as the only non-extractive approach for real-time monitoring of deep-dwelling organisms, it remains limited to species of prominent acoustic features, as well as local-level surveys. We employed omni-directional transmitters to emit wideband acoustic signals and produce a time-delay image of continuously moving targets. The swimming trajectories of sharks and other species of apex predatory megafauna were compared with ground truth data to establish potential indicators to identify species irrespective of backscatter. Repetitions were performed in a variety of environmental settings throughout the Mediterranean marine space of Israel and included species that are listed as data deficient (DD), endangered (EN), and critically endangered (CR) in this region. Our findings provide for the non-extractive, fishery-independent sampling of highly-migratory megafauna across large spatial scales.

6665: A recent risk assessment for chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) found some deepwater sharks were at relatively high risk of adverse impacts from fishing. Quantitative data for these species is limited, and some available information has been found to be unreliable. With a better understanding of spatial distributions, our knowledge of the risk to, and the status of these species would be more informed. This information would allow for the evaluation of potential stock boundaries, encourage comparisons of regional population structures, and overall, better inform fisheries management. Here, we investigate the suitability of several predictive modelling approaches, including vector-autoregressive spatio-temporal (VAST) models, to estimate spatio-temporal trends for seven deepwater sharks (Etmopterus granulosus, Centrophorus squamosus, Deania calcea, Centroselachus crepidater, Centroscymnus owstoni, Centroscymnus plunketi, and Dalatias licha) regularly caught in New Zealand deepwater trawl fisheries.

6666: The Western Central Atlantic (WCA) hosts a population of manta rays whose distribution and habitat preference is poorly understood to date. Obtaining this kind of information is crucial for effective conservation planning and implementation. In this study, we use ensemble ecological niche modelling (EENM) to predict the distribution of two sympatric manta ray species (Manta birostris and M. sp. cf birostris) in the WCA, and calculate the proportion of predicted suitable habitat that lies within protected areas. This technique has not been used to study the spatial ecology of manta rays at this scale before, but could prove to be a powerful tool in conservation planning. The EENM was developed combining 5,000 occurrence records derived from satellite tracking, diver observations, and verifiable social media posts. The predictions of the model indicate that suitable habitat for manta rays should be situated near the coast, in shallow and relatively warmer waters, especially near chlorophyll-α fronts. In the study region, key predicted suitable areas occur along the coasts of USA, Mexico, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Only 34% of predicted suitable habitat is encompassed by the present network of marine protected areas (MPAs), with just 0.2% in areas completely closed to fishing activities. The conservative life of oceanic manta rays makes this species sensitive to even moderate increases in mortality rates; for this reason, the existing MPAs may be likely to offer them little protection. As manta rays in the WCA are likely isolated from other populations worldwide, recolonization of the area following local extinction would be extremely unlikely and could even result in the loss of the endemic M. sp. cf birostris. Future conservation planning in the region should explicitly include conservation of manta rays in its targets, with particular focus on areas identified as key habitats for these species co-occurring in the WCA.

6667: A unique stronghold for the Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina) is found in the Canary Islands, where the species is still frequently encountered by divers and fishers. This provides a great opportunity to conduct research into Angelshark ecology, as limited understanding of Angelshark habitat use, movement and site fidelity at is a major factor preventing effective species protection and conservation. A key focus for Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI) (a collaborative initiative between Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Zoological Research Museum Alexander Koenig and Zoological Society of London) is the investigation of juvenile Angelshark habitat in the region and identification of Angelshark nursery areas. The definition of shark nursery areas varies greatly in scientific literature, but ASP:CI have developed a multidisciplinary approach (using citizen science sightings, satellite imagery, focal surveys and mark-recapture techniques) to test the three nursery area criteria outlined in Heupel et al. 2007. Research over the last four years has identified that juvenile Angelsharks are present across a number of shallow, sheltered beaches in the Canary Islands. The team have identified two confirmed nursery areas, 13 potential nursery areas and 21 beaches where juvenile Angelsharks are observed. Mark-recapture work at the largest confirmed nursery area, Playa de Las Teresitas in Tenerife, confirms that juvenile Angelsharks remain present for up to 15 months. Data were used to develop a Guidance Document on the identification and protection of juvenile Angelshark habitat in the Canary Islands, which identifies eight key recommendations to improve protection of these areas.

6668: Labial cartilages are paired structures located outside the jaws whose purpose in sharks is not completely clear yet. Labial cartilages vary a lot in current shark species, ranging from three pairs to a complete reduction, from massive to slender and from long to short. In our current work we used CT-images as a non-invasive method to check for labial cartilages in different shark species occupying different ecological niches and using different feeding strategies. The goal is to find out if the labial cartilages are a phylogenetic or an ecological trait. Therefore, we used nine species, which then were grouped according to their ecological niche into deep living, oceanic and benthic. We were able to detect that the labial cartilages in the oceanic species – especially in those known for ram-feeding behavior – were massively reduced while the ones in the benthic species were well conserved and strongly developed. Among the species classified by us as deep living we saw rather unique adaptations in the labial cartilages in comparison to the benthic group. For example, the cookie-cutter shark Isistius brasiliensis has very strong, fused labial cartilages and the ones of the frilled shark Chlamydoselachus anguineus are very slender. Therefore, we assume that the labial cartilages are an ecological trait and can give additional information on the feeding behavior in sharks and are also capable of giving information about the feeding behavior in extinct species, since labial cartilages were also detected in fossils. In future works we are going to check on as many species as possible to either confirm or refuse this theory. A phylogenetic signal was not discovered so far and the developmental basis of these structures still is ambiguous.

6669: Coastal top predators are exposed to a wide variety of nutrient and contaminant sources due to the diversity of trophic chains within coastal areas. Here we measured mercury (Hg) isotopes in two co-occurring shark species (the bull shark Carcharhinus leucas and the tiger shark Galeocerdo cuvier) and their prey from a coastal ecosystem of the Indian Ocean, to (i) determine the main Hg source for these marine predators and (ii) explore the relevance of mercury isotopes as tracers of diet composition and feeding habitat. As Hg is mainly found under the methylmercury form in shark and teleost fish muscle, Hg isotope signatures (Δ199Hg and δ202Hg) of shark prey suggested that bull sharks were exposed to methylmercury produced in the water column while tiger sharks were exposed to mesopelagic methylmercury with additional microbial transformation in shelf sediments. Δ199Hg values efficiently traced the ecology of the two predators, demonstrating that bull sharks targeted coastal prey in shallow waters while tiger sharks were mainly foraging on shelf species in deeper waters. Unexpectedly, we found a large positive shift in δ202Hg between sharks and their prey, leading to high δ202Hg values in the two shark species. The shift in δ202Hg strongly suggests that significant Hg demethylation occurs in sharks, representing a protective mechanism to limit the accumulation of methylmercury and its toxic effects.

6670: Global abundance of blue shark (Prionace glauca, L. 1758) has dramatically declined over the last 30 years, which is why, in some areas, this species has been categorized as "Critically Endangered" by the IUCN. Conservation and management of Mediterranean blue sharks (BS) suffer from a lack of knowledge regarding population structure and the dynamics of connectivity with contingents in the adjacent North-eastern Atlantic. Here, we filled in this knowledge gap by measuring genetic diversity and differentiation of BS individuals (N = 291) sampled across the Mediterranean Sea, and along the Atlantic continental slope of South- and North-western Europe, based on thousands of novel single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) developed through double-digest Restriction-site Amplified DNA (ddRAD) sequencing. SNP variation revealed a lack of genetic differences between Western and Eastern Mediterranean, and Mediterranean and North East Atlantic blue sharks, indicating the occurrence of a near- or full-panmixia across the North-eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Therefore, the Mediterranean BS population can be considered an extension of the North-eastern Atlantic population, which is in contrast with the current stock delineation and management. These results are in contrast also with long term tagging data, which suggest that the blue shark don't cross the Strait of Gibraltar. These contrasting results highlight the need to integrate multidisciplinary studies to better reveals the connectivity of higly mobile species, such as the blue shark, in order to take more appropriate conservation actions. Beyond the region's population structure, we envision that the developed SNPs could be exploited for the traceability of BS products globally (e.g. Atlantic vs Pacific), helping to tackle the major threat to BS populations, represented by the millions of unreported by-caught blue sharks, which enter the global fin trade each year.

6671: Cartilaginous fish represent less than 5% of marine fish species and in the Mediterranean Sea there are at least 79 species (45 shark species and 34 ray). Some sharks are considered apex predators and most of them are asynchronous opportunistic feeders. Predators play central role in marine and terrestrial environment. They exercise top-down control on lower trophic levels and compete one each other for same resources. Occasionally, opportunistic apex predators can attack another large predator (i.e. space competition). The Strait of Messina (central Mediterranean Sea) is a biodiversity hotspot thanks to its unique hydrodynamic regimes and host different shark species. In the last decade, several shark attacks over other predators in the Strait of Messina were documented between mainly in July. The attacked species were primarily swordfish (Xiphias gladius) but natural predation on giant devil ray (Mobula mobular) was also recorded. Generally, photos and video were taken after the harpooned swordfish were brought on board and are the only witness of these events. Indeed, most of the event stated here did happen after the animals were harpooned by feluca boats while swordfish (or other animals) were dead or life-fighting. These events were characterized by a well visible bite and removal of large muscle. The cause of the attacks most likely are associated to the weakness of the prey and the smell of blood and hormones released by injured fish. Since different species of shark inhabit the Strait of Messina, it is not really easy to identify shark species from the shape of the bite. There is also a lack of information and identification accuracy in species that inhabit or migrate through the Strait of Messina and therefore more research is needed to identify and monitor those highly mobile species and also to improve the knowledge on its behaviour.

6672: Pelagic sharks include oceanic and semi-oceanic species, and are mostly represented by the orders Carcharhiniformes, Lamniformes, and Squaliformes. Due to their complex life cycle, research on these organisms can be difficult in terms of logistic and finance. Because of this, the use of touristic operations and citizen science has been seen as an effective method to study these animals in areas where their abundance is significant. Due to the characteristics of the study area, we expect to find a high species richness, as well as seasonal patterns regarding relative abundance of sharks as a function of environmental factors. The main goal of this study was to create an inventory of pelagic shark species in Cabo San Lucas, and identify seasonal patterns in their abundance, as well as contribute data that supports the use of tourism on the study of pelagic species. To do this, submarine censuses were completed, registering shark species' richness, relative abundance, sex and size of the individuals, as well as environmental factors such as sea surface temperature, wind speed, cloudiness and depth (if possible). We observed 8 species during the censuses, with the most abundant being Carcharhinus falciformis, Sphyrna zygaena, and Isurus oxyrinchus. Also, we identified seasonal patterns on the relative abundance of the latter, where I. oxyrinchus was the most dominant species during the cold season (December-March), S. zygaena during the transitional period (April-June), and C. falciformis during the warm season (July-November). This is the first formal inventory of species done for the area, and we were able to demonstrate the viability of touristic operations and citizen science as tools used for the constant monitoring of these organisms and the establishment of baselines for these populations. This is especially important since these species are being taken advantage of by the growing nature tourism sector in Mexico.

6673: Difficulties in sampling large, mobile marine predators, such as great white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) have hindered the investigation of behaviour, but collaboration with ecotourism companies could offer an alternative data resource for scientific research. White Shark Africa (of Mossel Bay South Africa) volunteered data collected by their onboard crew during tourist excursions from 2009 through 2011, constituting of over 660 sampling hours and 985 individual shark sightings. The behaviour observed during each trip was used to assign each shark sighting to a 'behavioural state' (to encompass the overall behaviour of the shark on that trip), termed 'aggressive', 'cautious' and 'inquisitive'. Multiple explanatory variables related to weather, environment, seasonality, anthropic activity, conspecific presence and individual demographics were subjected to generalised linear models to identify variables which were significantly related to the presence of each behavioural state. Classification trees were used to analyse how significant variables affected white shark behaviours. Cautious behavioural state was found to be related to the order in which sharks arrived at the boat, the size of the shark and the bait type used. The probability of observing cautious behaviour was highest for sharks of smaller size (TL) which were first to arrive at the boat, and when baiting with tuna and snoek. Comparatively, aggressive behavioural state, was found to be related to running average minimum air temperatures (RTMIN) and arrival time. The probability of observing aggressive behaviour was highest during early morning sampling and when the RTMIN was low. Inquisitive behavioural state was also found to be significantly related to arrival time, but also to sea surface temperature (SST). The probability of observing inquistive behaviours was also highest during early morning sampling, but also when SST was warmer. Overall, modelling indicated that environmental conditions, anthropic activity, shark size and the presence of conspecifics all impacted on white shark behaviour. This study was the first to use ecotourism data in ethological research and the results indicate that collaboration with ecotourism operators could be invaluable for the collection of large, high-power data sets. Data sourced from ecotourism could be used in a wide array of scientific studies, as long as rigorous statistical methods are applied, and the results interpreted with consideration of the sampling methodology.

6674: The Top Predator laboratory of Morris Kahn Marine Research Station has been running a shark-tagging project in the last 4 years, as part of a long-term ecological research programme. The study takes place at an anthropogenic, seasonal aggregation area of sharks in the warm discharge waters of power plants along the Mediterranean coast of Israel. Following the tagging protocol of Sharklab (Bimini, Bahamas), 51 sharks have been tagged thus far, of which 35 were dusky sharks (Carcharhimus obscurus; 34 females and 1 male) and 16 sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus; all male). These species are listed by the IUCN as data deficient (DD) and endangered (EN) in the Mediterranean Sea, respectively. The tagging procedure includes morphometric measurements as well as DNA, stable isotopes, blood chemistry and microbiome sampling. All tagged sharks are issued a subcutaneous PIT tag as well as a spaghetti tag. 19 dusky sharks and 10 sandbar sharks were tagged with acoustic transmitters and an array of 11 receivers was placed within the tagging site and in other aggregation areas, such as offshore mariculture facilities, throughout Israel's marine space. Results indicate thermo-regulated fidelity at human-altered habitats and size as well as sex-dependent aggregating behaviour. In the Mediterranean Sea, where shark populations have declined dramatically over the last 70 years, Israeli waters have become an oasis for coastal sharks and a hub for their research, supported by ground-breaking conservation, legislation and enforcement.

6675: Acoustic telemetry is a well-established tool that has been used around the world for more than three decades to get an understanding of the spatio-temporal movements and associated behaviour of a wide range of aquatic animals. New emerging technologies are being developed continuously that allow for new research applications and designs. Examples for these new technologies are (1) real-time observations of both aquatic animals as well as their aquatic environment and (2) acoustic data storage tags. Applied real-time systems may consist of various underwater sensors, acoustic telemetry tags on aquatic animals, a surface hub that receives data from the sensors as well as from the tags, and a cloud-centric database. Such systems are now in use at several global installations. Data access is available via a mobile phone or laptop that provide real-time notifications when tagged animals are near receivers or the current state of environmental variables. Acoustic data storage tags might be used especially for far-ranging animals such as sharks and rays that might inhabit coastal and pelagic regions at different times of the year. These applications can be used to get a bigger picture of a species behaviour and its spatio-temporal distribution in order to address conservation and management measures since data is also collected while animals are outside of acoustic arrays. Here, we will explore the evolution of the use of acoustic telemetry and how receiving data in real-time and in acoustic data storage applications will help sustain our ocean ecosystems.

6676: Information like habitat preferences and trophic ecology regarding juvenile white sharks Carcharodon carcharias (WS) and shortfin mako sharks Isurus oxyrinchus (MS) is lacking. This study investigates the habitat use of juvenile MS and WS in the nursery area of Sebastian Vizcaino Bay (SVB) using stable isotope analysis in multiple tissues. During 2015 and 2016, we collected muscle (n=165), blood samples (n=147), red blood cells (RBC; n=62) and plasma (n=70) of young MS and muscle (n=6), RBC (=2) and plasma (n=2) of young WS. The size range for MS was 64.5-196 cm of total length (TL) and for WS it was 130-292 cm TL. Shortfin mako and white sharks had significant differences for muscle tissue in δ13C values (W = 255.5, p < 0.0001), but not in δ15N values (W = 1189.5, p = 0.08). We did not find significant differences in δ13C values (W = 228, p-value = 0.045) and δ15N values (W = 420.5, p-value = 0.8) of whole blood between shortfin mako and white sharks. In addition, sharks with similar TL of both species (MS > 102 cm TL and WS <186 cm TL) showed a similar pattern of δ15N values for whole blood, RBCs and plasma. MS and WS with similar total length (MS> 102 cm TL and WS < 186 cm TL) reflected in their tissues (muscle, blood, RBC and plasma) the regional baseline 15-N enriched isotopic signature of SVB, suggesting that SVB has a unique isotopic signature (isoscape). The similarity in isotopic niche and isotopic composition between shortfin mako and white sharks in multiple tissues reflecting large and short time periods suggest shared resource and common habitat use inside SVB throughout extended times confirming their residency in this area during their earlier life stages.

6677: Whale sharks are usually observed in coastal areas throughout the highly productive tropical and subtropical regions. The Indo-Pacific sub-population is declining mainly due to fisheries catches, bycatch and vessel strikes. Accordingly, in 2016 the species was assessed as "Endangered" on the IUCN Red List. Despite conservation concerns, there are still substantial gaps in the knowledge of whale shark ecology. This study investigates the temporal variability of whale shark presence in the South Ari Atoll Marine Protected Area (S.A.MPA). Even if the area is very limited (about 42km2) it appears to be an important aggregation site for the species in the Maldives archipelago. Since 2012 the Maldives Whale Shark Research Programme (MWSRP) has been collecting data year-round within the MPA. Due to the heterogeneity of the effort among different years only data collected between 2014 and 2017 has been considered in this study. A total of 572 sharks encounters have been reported in this period. Concurrently, in situ Sea Surface Temperature (SST) has also been collected. Sightings per Unit of Effort (SPUE) was calculated based on the number of survey trips carried out per month and per year during favorable environmental conditions (e.g. wind speed not exceed 3 in the Beaufort scale and partial and total clouds covered conditions). Generalized Linear Models have been used to analyse the temporal variability of the SPUE. No significant difference has been observed in SPUE across the study period. However, taking into consideration data on a monthly-year basis, the species' occurrence presents significant differences (P-level < 0.01). Further analysis revealed that SST could be a significant covariate. The understanding offered by this study provides additional information upon which to base an appropriate management strategy in the MPA for this wide-ranging species.

6678: The North Sea is known for its natural richness. Yet it is also one of most intensively exploited seas in the world, and, as a result, fish species have disappeared or populations are reduced to low numbers. There is a growing call to restore the natural richness of the North Sea but, it is often unclear what this is, because baseline studies date back 60 years at best. Elasmobranchs are an example of a group of species of which populations in the North Sea have marginalized over the past century. These includes the critically endangered angelshark Squatina squatina and common skate Dipturus intermedius. We review the historical abundance and some life-history aspects of these species in the Dutch marine waters using a variety of historical sources. Palaeontological sources dating back to the origin of the North Sea suggest that these species always have been present in the area. Written historical sources from the 16th to the 19th century suggest that the angelshark used to be fairly common and that the common skate was indeed common. Catch reports indicate that the angel shark started to decline at the onset of the 20th century and went locally extinct in the 1970s. Landings and fishery-independent data of common skate show a similar picture. The start of the decline coincides with the onset of steam-powered fisheries whereas the demise follows on the intensification of diesel-powered beam-trawlers. Historical reports and catch data indicates that angelsharks mainly visited the area in summer to reproduce. Common skates were mainly caught in winter and these were mostly young individuals that supposedly used the area as nursery grounds. Our study shows that if we base our ideas of a North Sea ecosystem on a baseline view after 1900 we may have overly low expectations of its potential natural richness.

6679: The decline of elasmobranch populations in the Mediterranean Sea highlights the need of developing effective management strategies. The biological traits of such organisms include internal fertilization, hence decoupling mating from egg release/parturition, a longer life and a slower growth rate compared to most teleosts, making elasmobranch populations particularly vulnerable to fishery exploitation. Because of their biology, these species distribution may vary drastically among life stages (e.g. adults vs juveniles, pregnant vs non-pregnant females) and sexes. Movements across Mediterranean water bodies, between mating, parturitions, feeding areas and the occurrence of aggregations in a specific area are fundamental points for understanding their ecology. Therefore, integrating movement information in management strategies of these species is a crucial step forward. Such data on pelagic and benthic species are scarce throughout the Mediterranean Sea and especially in the Adriatic Sea. In this study, we adopted a conventional tagging approach in the Adriatic Sea using "spaghetti" tags in collaboration with professional and recreational fishermen, elasmobranchs, caught as target or bycatch, were tagged and released after species identification, recording size, sex and maturity (for males by clasper calcification and for females TL50 was used if known) and storing release coordinates in Tshark.org database. So far, we tagged 592 individuals (12 species) among which the majority are smooth-hound sharks (Mustelus mustelus and M. punctulatus), eagle ray (Myliobatis aquila) and pelagic sting ray (Pteroplatytrygon violacea). We received 6 recapture reports out of 301 of tagged Mustelus spp, ranging between 6 months to 5 days after release, and 1 of pelagic sting ray, after 2 months and 15 days after release. The longest distance recoded was of 20 nautical miles (NM) for Mustelus spp and 125 NM for P. violacea. As this approach relies on the recapture reporting, the collaboration between research institutions across Mediterranean countries, and between researchers and fishermen as well, is fundamental to increase recapture information.

6680: Elasmobranchs constitute a target or bycatch of a wide variety of fishing techniques. Such anthropogenic pressure has brought to a drastic reduction of local populations across the Mediterranean Sea. Moreover, limited-data collection and species misidentification, among others, have led to a scarcity of historical data on species occurrence and abundance trends in several taxa. Such information is particularly valuable to study migration dynamics and behaviour variations, as well as to reconstruct historical trends. To fill this data gap, the use of local ecological knowledge from professional fishermen can be considered as a valuable source of semi-quantitative information on several aspects of species ecology, abundance and behavioural aspects. Through a questionnaire survey, fishermen operating with diverse fishing gears such as bottom and pelagic trawlers, set nets and longlines were interviewed by trained researchers with the aid of photo-identification materials. A total of 211 interviews were collected across nine Mediterranean FAO-GSA sub-areas (9, 10, 11, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 28). Results covered a wide range of elasmobranch species with regard to coastal, pelagic and deep-sea environment. Interviewers indicated species that were abundant in the past, declined recently and showed size variation compared to past catches. Moreover, fishermen reported aggregation sightings/events, seasonal movements and species-specific fishing area. The present study constitutes a baseline regarding abundance and distribution of elasmobranch species in historical times and may represent a valuable tool for data deficient taxa. It also gives new insights on elasmobranchs behavioural and ecological aspects and highlights priority species and suitable geographic areas for conservation and behavioural studies.

6681: It is known that juveniles whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) have tendency to gather, seasonally, in a few coastal areas around the world to feed on zooplankton; however little is known about their food preferences. The CSS (Centro Studi Squali) scientific coordinator of the project "Whale shark feeding ecology" (in partnership with University of Calabria, University of Siena, ISPRA, University of Naples Federico II, Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn), in 2016, started the study of these aggregations. During field observations we collected zooplankton samples and we observed feeding behaviour of sharks to understand the main characteristics of the zooplankton community that appears to cause said gatherings. So far two expeditions (2017 and 2018) have been carried out in the channel of Mozambique, in the coastal waters of the Nosy Be (MG). Here whale sharks are present in the last four months of the year: data were collected in the eastern part of the island in late November-early December which is the peak season for whale shark sightings in the area. Zooplankton samples were collected vertically from 10 m depth to surface, using a net with 200 µm mesh aperture. The samples were concentrated using a 50µm filter and fixed with alcohol (70%) and lugol (1%). At the same time, location, water temperature and transparency, shark presence/absence and feeding behaviour were recorded. Quantitative and qualitative analysis of zooplankton samples were performed at Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn and ISPRA laboratories. We calculated zooplankton biomass and abundance. We identified at species level the most important zooplanktonic taxa (copepods, chetognats etc) and moreover we calculated their size spectra.

6682: The knowledge of Hexanchus vitulus (Springer & Waller, 1969) and other deep-sea sharks in the Caribbean Sea is considered scarce, as these species are unfrequently captured by local artisanal fishers and therefore scientific research regarding its biology has not been developed. The present study reports the first record with morphometry data of H. vitulus in this area, in order to provide useful information for future comparisons of specimens in other coastal regions. A total of ten Atlantic six gill sharks was captured offshore El Quetzalito, Guatemala (15.740379 N, -88.274621W) by artisanal fishers at using longlines and fishing nets at a depth of 275-365 m. The date of capture, fishing gear, used bait, sex, total length, precaudal length, and fork length were registered from each shark. Taxonomic identification was carried out through the description published by Compagno et al., (2005) and Daly-Engel et al., (2018). All the specimens were identified as H. vitulus due to the presence of six gills, a slender body with brown dorsal and white ventral coloration, narrow head and mouth, anterior serrations on lower teeth, and large eyes. These characteristics are the same described for H. nakamurai, because H. vitulus has been describes as a cryptic species with no evident external differentiation known to date. The length of the specimens ranged between 61-165 cm TL, with a mean of 142 ± 29 SD cm TL. Most of the captured sharks were considered mature individuals with the exception of a juvenile female caught in 2015. Sex ratio of this sample was 2.3:1 (Males:Females), where 90% of the sharks were mature individuals. The high quantity of mature sharks in this sample differs from what observed in other relatively close areas like Belize. Arguments regarding a potential segregation between mature and immature individuals related to locality and month are presented.

6683: The ecology of mantas and echeneids in the Eastern Tropical Pacific is poorly understood. In this study we describe the frequency of interactions between the vulnerable Mobula birostris and its symbiont Remora remora, through the participation of scientists and tourists in a marine protected area. Data were obtained by the analysis of underwater pictures of observed mantas with remoras during 139 diving days at sea during the years 2016-2017. A total of 273 records of mantas with remoras was registered from 207 identified individuals. Estimated size of mantas ranged from 250-550 cm DW, with an average size of 380 ± 50 cm SD. Sex ratio of mantas was 1.3:1 (Female:Male) as observed from our sample of 89 females (42.9%), 68 males (32.8%), and 50 individuals (24%) for which sex could not be determined. The remora species observed in all the mantas was the common remora Remora remora. Average number of remoras attached to the mantas was 1.6 ± 0.56 remoras per manta. Estimated size of the remora ranged between 40-80 cm TL, with an average of 60 cm ± 10 cm SD. During the study period, there were no significant differences between months and the number of remoras per manta (H7,271=5.13; p=0.64). Most of the mantas usually had one or two remoras, 43 % (n=117) and 53.5 % (n=147), respectively; while 2.5% of the mantas (n=5) were observed with three remoras, and only two individuals with four (0.9%). Although a higher number of remoras in female mantas was observed, there was no significant differences according to the morphotype or sex of the mantas (H3,208=7.90; p=0.04) confirmed by the Bonferroni post-hoc test. The study of this host-symbiont interaction is discussed in terms of the potential insights that this kind of research could provide regarding the ecology of mantas and remoras if compared with other aggregation sites.

6684: In the years 2017, 2018 and 2019 the feeding behavior of the whale shark has been studied off Nosy Be Island (Madagascar). In particular, the investigations involved the description of the behavioral modules of the whale shark and their relationship with the phytoplankton communities. In total, 65 phytoplankton samples were collected in the following four behavioural conditions: 0 - absence of whale sharks; 1 - presence of swimming whale sharks; 2 - presence of whale sharks in horizontal feeding; 3 - presence of whale sharks in vertical passive feeding; 4 - presence of whale sharks in vertical active feeding. All samples were immediately filtered and then frozen to be subsequently analyzed by HPLC to identify the total biomass and contribution of the different functional groups of phytoplankton. In total 8 phytoplanctonic taxa have been identified: Prasinophyceae, Dinoflagellata, Cryptophyceae, Primnesiophyceae, Pelagophyceae, Chlorophyceae, Cyanobacteria and Bacillariophyceae. Among them, Cryptophyceae were the most abundant. Our results seemed to highlight a certain correlation also between behavioral feeding intensity exhibited by sharks and the total biomass of phytoplancton. In particular, this appeared more evident with some groups of algae that might be involved in the release of the dimethyl sulfonio propionate (DMSP). This substance is produced by algal organisms in response to predation by zooplankton organisms. Since DMSP is a substance characterized by a strong odor, the results could demonstrate the fundamental role of smell in the identification of food sources by the whale shark, as confirmed for marine birds.

6685: Despite in recent years the interest about the human-made noise effects on marine animals have received notably increasing, at date few studies have investigated the potential role of acoustic masking on animal's bio-ecological relationship. In this study, we exposed twelve specimens of small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula, Linnaeus 1758) to biological and anthropogenic sounds in order to assess their behavioural changes potentially referable to pray presence and masking effect due to the shipping noise. Specifically, the sharks held individually in aquarium were exposed to three acoustic experimental conditions differentiated in their spectral (Hz) components (biological and anthropogenic mixed sources) and intensity (dB re 1 µPa) levels. Swimming behaviour and spatial distribution of the specimens were recorded. The results highlighted significant differences in time spent in swimming and in spatial use of the aquarium among the experimental conditions. The sharks concentrated their swimming behaviour in the aquarium's lower sections when the intensity levels of the biological acoustic sources were higher than the anthropogenic ones. Conversely, when the intensity levels of the anthropogenic sources were higher than the biological, the specimens showed the highest values of time spent in swimming, and changed their spatial distribution highlighting an aquarium occupancy in favour of the less noisy sections. In conclusion, in this study was hypothesised that the environmental soundscape could play an important role in the small-spotted catshark prey-predator relationship and that the impact of masking effect can strictly depends on the acoustic intensity levels.

6686: The worldwide abundance of Galeus melastomus in the biological composition of fishery bycatch led to consider this species as a key-taxon for understanding the mysterious biology and ecology of sharks living in deep ecosystems. With the present work, we aim to unravel the population structure of the blackmouth catshark in the Mediterranean Sea and adjacent North-Eastern Atlantic with the use of nuclear molecular markers (simple sequence repeats, SSRs) and compare our results with recent findings based on mitochondrial DNA supporting total panmixia in the species. Given the absence of species-specific microsatellite markers we attempted the cross-amplification of a panel of 129 SSRs developed for Centroselachus crepidater, Galeorhinus galeus, Hexanchus griseus, Mustelus antarcticus, M. canis, M. henlei, M. mustelus, Negaprion brevirostris, Scyliorhinus canicula, Squalus acanthias and S. mitsukurii on blackmouth catsharks collected during scientific surveys undertaken in different years. The rationale of the chosen methodology was based on the calculation of genetic distances between NADH2 sequences (1044bp long) derived from 595 species of elasmobranchs. Our strategy focused on testing first SSRs markers developed on closely-related species. Then, we assessed highly polymorphic markers developed on non-closely-related species. After a pilot gradient amplification on few individuals from three different geographic macro-areas, we screened a total of 24 samples at the established conditions. To date, 16 microsatellite loci have been classified as potential candidates for the successful cross-amplification on Atlantic and Mediterranean samples of G. melastomus. These candidate loci will be applied in the population genetic analysis delineated in the Atlantic Ocean (two sites) and in the Mediterranean Sea (five sites). Hopefully, the higher resolution power of the markers chosen for this study will be able to disclose any signal of genetic structure of the blackmouth catsharks and will contribute to improve the knowledge on deep-sharks.

6687: According to Boldrocchi et alii (2017) the information on the diet of white sharks in the Mediterranean inferred from stomach content analyses of 103 stomachs revealed among other prey items 45 bony fish and 5 cartilaginous fish. The most common teleost prey groups were tuna (Thunnus spp.) and swordfish (Xiphias gladius). In the Strait of Messina motorboats known as "feluche" or are used to catch the swordfish. These have a 20-25 m high mast, on the top of which sighters and helmsmen are placed: on the front there is a walkway up to 45 m long, at the end of which the harpooner is standing. In this sector of the sea, the press often reports the presence of large sharks. In the present note we report three shark attacks (documented by photographs) on Red Tuna and Swordfish in the Strait. On April 5, 2017, during the ascent of a 70 kg line-caught red tuna, a white shark launched an attack that documented a bite that removed about 30 kg of flesh from the ventral region. The second attack took place on August 1, 2019 in the water in front of S. Agata of Messina on a swordfish hooked by a feluca, "Felicia II"; the swordfish after being harpooned fell to the sea bottom at a depth 80 metres, where it remained for about 20 minutes. Subsequently the fish it was set on board allowing to record a bite that ha detached about 20 kg of flesh, the entire weight of the fish was estimated at around 107 kg. The third attack was observed by the same fishermen on August 5, 2019. A swordfish swimming below the surface was successfully attacked by a white shark which cut off its tail. The same swordfish was subsequently harpooned and hoisted on board on the feluca.

6688: Despite Calabria represents an interesting study area due to its geographic position, nothing is known of the presence of sharks and rays in this region. Data presented in this work come from nineteen years of opportunistic fishing surveys (from 2000 to 2019). Our data shows that 53 species of elasmobranchs are present in Calabrian seas: 30 of these are sharks, 22 are rays. To these, 1 species of Chimaeras must be added. All they represent about the 50% of species reported for the Mediterranean. The more widespread encountered species were Hexanchus griseus, Scyliorhinus canicula, Prionace glauca, Raja asterias and Raja clavata. Very interesting is also the presence and distribution in the study area of species such as Cetorhinus maximus, Carcharodon carcharias, Isurus oxyrhincus, Sphyrna zygaena and Mobula mobular. Also, information on localities and specimens has been presented. We report also new records of Alopias superciliosus, Carcharhinus obscurus and Sphyrna mokarran.

6689: The deep-sea can be defined as the part of the oceans below 200 meters. The organisms living there can be qualified as deep-sea organisms. However, a lot of these organisms display vertical movements bringing them above 200 meters, making it difficult to classify them. Deep-sea organisms are thus considered here to be organisms spending most of their life cycle below 200 meters. Due to the technical difficulties linked to deep-sea study, a lot remains to be discovered about the organisms living in the depths of the oceans. The trophic structure and interactions inside the deep-sea food-webs remain poorly known for a lot of taxa, including deep-sea sharks. Here, we first try to separate the known shark species between deep-sea and surface species. We then try to review the available knowledges on deep-sea sharks' diet. Most of the information come from stomach contents but the use of more recent techniques is increasing in order to assess deep-sea sharks' trophic ecology. Stable isotope analyzes and fatty acid profiles have proved to provide useful information in this regard and have been included in our review.

6690: Environmental factors have an important effect on sharks. It has been observed that the horizontal and vertical movements of these animals, as well as their distribution, abundance, and use of habitat, can be influenced by biotic and abiotic factors. Due to the fact that pelagic sharks possess specific environmental preferences, and the area of Cabo San Lucas is characterized by drastic oceanographic variability between the warm and temperate seasons, we expect the relative abundance of these organisms to be influenced by environmental factors, especially temperature and chlorophyll concentration. The main goal of this study was to determine which environmental and temporal variables (month and hour) have significant influence over the relative abundance of Carcharhinus falciformis and Sphyrna zygaena in Cabo San Lucas. To do this, submarine censuses were completed, where we registered the relative abundance of these species, as well as environmental factors such as sea surface temperature, wind speed, and water color. Also, satellite data regarding chlorophyll a concentration was downloaded. These variables were incorporated into generalized linear models (GLM), where the relative abundance was the response factor. For C. falciformis, we found significant differences for temperature, chlorophyll concentration, month of the year, and hour (GLM, p<0.001). Its relative abundance was greater with warm waters (29.7±0.3ºC), whereas it was lower with high concentrations of chlorophyll (0.15±0.002 mg/m3). Also, they were more abundant during Autumn and between 5 and 6 pm. In contrast, water color was the only variable that showed significant differences for S. zygaena (GLM, p<0.01), with green water resulting in greater relative abundance. This is the first study to characterize the abundance and temporality of two highly exploited shark species in the region, and we found differences amongst them. Our results give valuable information in terms of management and conservation efforts in the area.

6691: Since 2000, the CSS team (Sharks Studies Center), as part of the project: "Ecology and Ethology of the Great White Shark", has been collecting ethological data during Scientific Expeditions organized in South Africa in Gansbaai, 200 km east of Cape Town. In Gansbaai Bay and around Dyer Island and Geyser rock, there is a large population of White Sharks that can be observed thanks to the support of local ecotourism operators authorized to reach the best field observation sites. Research activities about ethological and ecotoxicological analyses, covered between 2003 and 2019, were developed in collaboration with: University of Calabria and Siena in Italy and Stellenbosch University in South Africa. In order to enable proper data collection, it was necessary to develop techniques to identify white sharks that consist mainly of the collection of various biometric and environmental data in special sheets, as well as photographs of animals with special attention to the dorsal fins. After the first years of optimization of the techniques and of staff involved, it was necessary to identify the individual specimens and, between 2009 and 2019, it was possible to create a db. Since 2009 to 2019, between march and may, 423 different white sharks were catalogued for a total of 440 hours of field observations from the boat and 220 hours of observations from the cage, including 99 photographs of unique dorsal fins. In this work the preliminary results, related to the trends of the population present in Gansbaai Bay are presented and discussed.

6692: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are known to have large-scale implications over entire ecosystems, however, their effects over key predators, such as elasmobranchs, are still poorly understood. Although multiples studies have revealed several developmental, physiological, and behavioural implications of temperature increase in this group, this has yet to be addressed in an MHW context. In the present study, we investigated the effects of a simulated MHW over the foraging behaviour of juvenile temperate sharks (Scyliorhinus canicula). Treatment conditions were chosen to reflect a realist MHW scenario based on previous events detected in the wild (15 days, Δ 3 °C above climatological normal; category II). Following exposure, the animal food intake, foraging motivation and response to both olfactory and electrical cues were assessed. While no changes were observed in food intake, cue response, and foraging time, there was an increase in the number of turns and biting events. These behavioural changes may indicate changes in foraging efficiency, which not only have the potential to undermine the coping capacity of shark juveniles but also to induce changes in the predation dynamics. As anthropogenic climate change continues unabated, MHWs are expected to increase in frequency, duration and intensity, which may further challenge the foraging efficiency of these key predators, with potential cascading consequences in ecosystems already subjected increasing pressure.

6693: From 2005 to 2018 the individual surface behaviour of bait-attracted white sharks during ecotourism activites has been studied off Dyer Island Nature Reserve (South Africa). Observations were made from a commercial cage-diving boat both by observers and by a drone. A total of 235 white sharks has been identified. The individual behavioural units observed were: parading, bait following, visual inspection, breach, tail slap, tail stand, spy hop, repetitive aerial gaping, and head-up vertical emerging. We compared the exhibition of these behaviors and the complexity of the ethograms to both biological (sex, age) and environmental (tides, cloud cover, underwater visibility, sea surface conditions, temperature, time of the day) factors. We observed no correlation between behavior and sex of the white sharks, while a significant correlation was observed comparing ethograms of mature and immature white sharks: young sharks performed more complex ethograms with a higher number of behavioural units than adult ones. Regarding the effects of environmental conditions, the sequence and structure of individual behaviors were affected in particular by cloud cover and tides.

6694: Since 1998, a public basking shark sightings recording scheme is established in French waters. The aim is to gather simple data on occurrences to locate any sightings hotspots and, in the long term, to detect possible variations in spatial and seasonal distribution of the sightings. Highlighting such areas could help to minimize conflict between this species of conservation concern and human activities. This type of projects involving members of the public are recognised for contributing also in terms of public awareness. This is something important to make possible the implementation of new measures to better protect basking sharks. We analysed data collected between 1998 and 2017 (20 years). 1857 sightings representing 2409 sharks were recorded. Data were analysed in term of spatial, inter-annual and seasonal distribution. Inter-annual and seasonal distribution were investigated globally and for several geographical areas (Mediterranean Sea, Bay of Biscay, Celtic Sea, Channel and south North Sea).

6695: White sharks are usually defined as generalist predators, with a well described ontogenetic dietary shift that occurs between the subadult and adult stages. Yet the majority of published studies have focused on large and mature individuals, so the information about feeding habits is still lacking for young white sharks. It is imperative to improve information about the trophic ecology of white sharks across life-stages to better understand habitat shifts and their early life movements inside nursery areas, which are determined by resources availability. This study provides the first insight into the trophic ecology of young white sharks using stable isotopes analysis (SIA) in muscle tissues to characterize prey contributions and ontogenetic changes in habitat use. We collected muscle of 21 white sharks from Sebastian Vizcaino Bay (SVB) during the period 2015-2018, including five newborns, three YOY and three juveniles. White shark isotopic values did not vary by sex (δ15N values: W = 52, p = 0.8 and δ13C values: t = 0.25, p = 0.8) as well as age classes (δ15N values: W =54, p = 0.4 and δ13C values: t = -0.9, p = 0.4) and we did not find variation based on size classes for δ13C and δ15N. However, we found changes in prey composition across white shark life stages, with significant changes throughout ontogeny. Mixing model indicate a high use of coastal areas for foraging, which likely represents the shift from the embryo's typical maternally-derived isotopic signature incorporated in offshore foraging regions to the postpartum isotopic composition, incorporated by neonates from inshore nursery habitats, including SVB. This study reinforces the assertion that coastal areas, like SVB and the prey preferences that take place in this area (from previous research) are critical for the development and to the successful foraging of young white sharks, providing relevant knowledge regarding this species.

6696: Three species of lantern sharks occur in Angolan waters: Etmopterus polli, E. pusillus, and E. spinax, along the continental slope at depths down to 1000 m. As part of the regional cooperation between Norway and Angola annual surveys were carried out on board the R/V Dr Fridtjof Nansen. During these surveys, 4162 individuals were collected, Total length (TL), sex, maturity and stomach content were recorded. The specimen's length range was: 10 to 27 cm TL for E. polli, 10 to 55 cm TL for E. pusillus and 10 to 35 cm TL for E. spinax. Food items were identified to the lowest possibly taxon, weighed, measured and grouped into three taxonomic groups: teleosts, cephalopods, crustaceans and remains (e.g. squid beaks, scales and otoliths). Prey importance was evaluated by using the index of relative importance (IRI), expressed as percentage (%IRI). To determine if there were significant differences in stomach contents between sexes and maturity stages, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) were done. The dependent variable used was the Index of Relative Fullness (IRF). Preliminary results show that these species consumed a relatively wide range of prey items belonging to three major groups: teleosts (10 families), crustaceans (7 families), and cephalopods (4 families). For all three Etmopterus species, cephalopods were the most frequent prey. The other categories varied in importance in the diet by species and life history stage. There were no significant differences in the diet of males and females, but we found an ontogenetic dietary shift, reflected in the importance of teleosts between immature and mature specimens. E. polli had the highest dietary diversity and seem to feed mainly on fast moving prey. This study provides the first quantitative investigation of the diets of three species of sharks belonging to the Etmopteridae family off Angola.
6697: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) such as organochlorine compounds (OCs) are still exploited in some countries both for special permit and for the non-regulation of these products. Marine apex predators like sharks have the potential to accumulate and biomagnify OCs due to their position in the trophic food web. In this study we analyzed hexachlorobenzene (HCB), dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane and its metabolites (DDTs) and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in 59 muscle samples from by-caught and free ranging sharks of 6 different species collected in 3 different areas: Mediterranean Sea, northern New South Wales (Australia) and Dyer Island (South Africa). Overall, South African specimens were the most impacted by PCBs and Mediterranean species by DDTs. Nevertheless, ratio between pp'DDE/pp'DDT in South African sharks suggested a recent use of this xenobiotic along with DDT fingerprint in Australian specimens, while unusually high values of op' DDT isomers are probably linked to the use of an industrial (non-insecticidal) DDT.

6698: Classified as vulnerable to near-threatened on the IUCN red list, the silky shark, Carcharhinus falciformis is a pelagic species. The species is vulnerable to overfishing due to its spatial distribution and biological characteristic. Using data from French and Spanish tropical tuna purse seine fishery, this study proposes a new method to derive an abundance index for silky shark's populations in two areas of the Indian Ocean. Two models were used: the first one describes the dynamics of sharks associated to floating objects (FOBs) used by tuna purse seiners in a social and in a non-social case. The second one illustrates the exchanges of individuals between the FOB-associated population and an external pool of sharks. The parameters estimated of the first model were obtained with fitting analysis. They were then integrated to the second model, allowing to derive an abundance index for the silky shark in statistical units of space and time and therefore the construction of temporal series of the population trend. This methodology has the potential to be applied to many other species associating with FOBs and serve as a tool for fisheries management.

6699: Deepwater species are in general more difficult to study compared to species in shallower waters due to the difficulty of access. This is limiting many studies to determining the presence and population composition at a very specific timepoint only, that is, the timepoint of catch, usually via a trawl. The power of such data therefore lies in the establishment of time series with many repeated measurements over a long time span, ideally also covering a large enough spatial area to capture the entire population range. We analysed >30 years of survey data from the Institute of Marine Research in Norway spanning minaly the North Sea and the Norwegian Sea focussing on deepsea sharks, skates and chimaera. We focussed on annual or bi-annual survey series that have been ongoing for at least 25 years. All survey series are designed to monitor the population status of commercial species like redfish, greenland halibut and shrimps and are based on trawl catches. Species-specific distributions, and changes over time, can be detected, as well as developments of population composition (e.g. size and gender) by such time series. However, critical information like presence/absence and continuous distribution along different habitat types are typically not possible to assess, and neither are "realistic" number for species not typically caught in trawls. We would like to present a few discussion points about the pro's and con's for dedicated chondrichthyan surveys and possible methodological additions to existing surveys, including the critical question about cost/benefit for e.g. rare, threatened or indicator species.
