6700: Marine contamination is worse than ever. To have an indication of stress or susceptibility, understanding how contamination correlates with key biological endpoints is essential. Sharks tend to accumulate high amounts of contaminants throughout their lives, bioaccumulating pollutants present in the water and biomagnifying the pollutants from their prey. Many shark species are caught and consumed all over the world, making them relevant for economical and public health reasons. To understand possible consequences of contamination, the present work aimed to quantify the levels of some metals in Scyliorhinus canicula and also measure biochemical biomarkers related with oxidative stress and energy metabolism. Moreover, efforts were made towards understating how the contamination-response patterns varied between lethal and less-invasive/non-lethal sampling. Sharks caught off the coast of Portugal by a commercial trawling boat were sampled. For each individual, levels of 13 metals were measured in both skin and muscle, while biochemical parameters were measured in several tissues including muscle, liver, blood and skin. Arsenic (As), iron (Fe), and zinc (Zn) had the higher mean values of all measured metals. There was a tendency for higher metal accumulation in skin, with differences being found between life-stages and genders. Furthermore, some analysed sharks surpassed stipulated guideline limits for human consumption of mercury (Hg) and As. Regarding the biochemical responses, suitable biomarker candidates could be identified as several significant correlations were observed between the physiological parameters and contaminant accumulation levels. When comparing lethal and non-lethal sampling some promising similarities were observed, especially when using skin biopsies, indicating good potential for being used as proxy for deeper tissues in future biomonitoring efforts. This study further highlights the effectiveness of combining biochemical parameters and pollutant body burden determinations to assess effects of contamination and demonstrates the great potential of sharks to be used in biomonitoring studies of the marine environment.

6701: Overexploitation is the primary cause of fish extinction risk, yet individual species declines are difficult to track, particularly in the high seas. This knowledge gap impedes progress towards Aichi Biodiversity Targets and Sustainable Development Goals. We take advantage of newly available timeseries for 53 timeseries of 18 species of oceanic sharks and rays to measure changes in abundance by calculating the Living Planet Index. Worldwide, the abundance of oceanic sharks and rays has declined by 71% since 1970, with the steepest ongoing decline occurring in the Indian Ocean. Recent catch quotas, prohibitions, and international trade regulations provide some hope, yet without a drastic improvement in implementation of management there is a real risk of worldwide collapse of these populations and a disruption of their ecological function.

6702: We analyzed the concentration of cadmium in the mesopredator Mustelus henlei in an area influenced by a natural deposit of phosphorite and by coastal upwellings. Both processes provide Cd in a natural way. In the Las Barrancas, Mexico, M. henlei is one of the most important coastal sharks in the artisanal fishery of the region, representing an important source for human consumption. Due to the risk that it may constitute for human health, it is necessary to know the concentrations of Cd in muscle and liver, the risk to consumers and evaluate the biomagnification of this element in the trophic chain. The concentrations of Cd in the muscle of M. henlei were lower than the limits of detection, then the meat of this species does not constitute a risk to human health. However, the liver hade average concentrations of 0.96 µg g-1 (0-6.07, min-max), these values are above what is established by the official Mexican Norm, probably due to the high influence of the phosphorite deposits present, and to the upwelling events in the study area. The Mann-Whitney U test showed that had statistically significant differences in Cd between females 0.65 µg g-1 (0.26-4.85, min-max) and males 1.21 µg g-1 (0.43-6.07, min-max): this is probably ta consequence of the metabolic characteristics of each sex. The linear regression showed that there was no relationship between the length of M. henlei and the Cd concentration: this let speculate that probably there is no bioaccumulation of the Cd in the liver as the organisms increase in size. The analysis of Cd in the main prey of M. henlei using the factor of biomagnification (FBM) indicated that red crab (P. planipes) with respect to M. henlei was: FBM= 1.08; whereas the chub mackerel (S. japonicus) was 4.57, which indicates a higher biomagnification of this element in chub mackerel.

6703: Oceanic manta rays Mobula birostris, are broadly distributed in tropical and temperate waters and their populations are in decline worldwide. In the Mexican Pacific Ocean, they are protected from fishing activity, with a permanent ban for their capture, possession and commerce in the whole country. For this reason, data on their ecology and toxicology must be obtained in non-invasive ways and the biopsies taken from free-ranging animals are a useful tool for toxicological studies. Data on persistent organochlorines (OCs) in sharks and rays are scarce, in manta rays are unknown. Occupying a low trophic level, manta rays could be an early sentinel for the contamination levels in the area. Although many of these persistent organic pollutants are nowadays banned in many countries of the world because of their negative effects on wildlife, they are still found in the environment due to their persistence and slow degradation. Concentrations of OCs such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and organochlorine pesticides (OCPs) were determined in skin and muscle biopsies of free-ranging oceanic manta rays in Revillagigedo Archipelago and Banderas Bay, where they aggregate in the Mexican Pacific Ocean. Biopsies were taken during scuba and freediving using a pole spear and underwent chemical extraction and subsequent analysis with a gas chromatograph equipped with mass spectrometer (GC-MS) to identify and quantify individual PCB congeners and OCPs. PCBs were detected in biopsies, while no OCPs were detected in any sample. This is the first time that persistent organochlorines are investigated in manta rays and represent a baseline for future studies. OCs can interfere with reproduction in fish and could pose a serious threat to the vulnerable populations of oceanic manta rays around the world.

6704: Humans, in addition to represent a direct threat to sharks, also indirectly exerts a strong pressure on these animals, due to the continuous release of polluting elements in the water and the atmosphere. Sharks, as predators at the top of marine food chain, act as final receptors for a series of polluting elements that are regularly discharged into the sea. The goal of this research was to delineate and compare trace elements concentration rates in vertebrae, skin and liver of a population of lesser spotted dogfish, Scyliorhinus canicula, from Central Mediterranean. 75 sharks were collected in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 12 miles off of Rocchette Punta Ala. 46 trace elements were analyzed in 75 vertebrae, 12 livers and 12 pieces of skin. Vertebrae were processed with LA-ICPMs, while liver and skin through acid attacks combined with ICPMs. The most abundant and potentially toxic elements were: lead, arsenic, manganese, zinc, nickel, copper, cadmium and iron. Lead, arsenic and manganese showed highest concentrations in the vertebrae, due to the diet of the sharks that is composed of crustaceans, bony fish and shellfish that accumulate many of these elements. Iron and nickel showed highest concentrations in the skin of the samples, due to their presence in the water column, especially along the coast where sharks were collected. At the end, cadmium, zinc and copper showed highest concentrations in the liver, due to their ability to induce trace elements binding metallothionein (MT), which chelates trace metals and reduce the concentration of cadmium.

6705: Elasmobranchs are among the most successful vertebrates in the Phanerozoic, with a stratigraphic distribution ranging from the Silurian to Recent times and a global distribution. Like other vertebrates, they share the use of bioapatite in making mineralized tissues. Bioapatite represents a unique archive of physical and chemical environmental information. Indeed, bioapatite lattice can accommodate iso- and hetero-valent substitutions during life or after burial and diagenesis, with a variation of the chemical composition during geological time. Chemical and crystal-chemical data can be achieved by different analytical tools, like laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS). As LA-ICPMS results are affected by physical-chemical preperties of the sample matrix, an internal standard is usually required to correct and validate the analytical results. Unluckily, an exclusive internal standard is so far missing for bioapatite, strongly affected by isomorphic sobstitutions. A possible solution can be the calibration with external standards which, however, are not so diffused. We propose herein a new method to prepare home-made matrix-matched calibration standards to measure major element concentrations. The method has been tested on living and fossil shark teeth. The final goal is the development of a reliable tool for chemical characterization by LA-ICPMS on small sized samples, avoiding the use of electron microprobe, that is considered a more appropriate technique, but which is more expensive, less diffused and, in any case, once again strictly dependent on the calibrating standards. Our technique can be useful to study teeth of living elasmobranchs in order to find possible chemical and crystal-chemical variation in bioapatite related, for example, to specific habitat, age, gender, etc.

6706: Both trace elements and isotopes analysis were performed on two samples of vertebrae of White Sharks Carcharodon carcharias from Favignana Island (Sicily, central Mediterranean). For the trace elements analysis, the ICP-MS associated by Laser Ablation allowed us to find 36 trace elements. More samples were taken, on the same vertebrae, along a transect that goes from the most central part of the vertebra to the distal one. Among these 36 trace elements we have been detected high concentrations of Pb, Fe, Zn, Sr, Ba and U. Fluctuations of these elements can be caused by different kind of processes such as variations in temperature, nutrition, uptake of urban pollutants and proximity to industrial areas. The stable isotopes (δ15N and δ13C) analysis has been performed through IRMS (Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry) and allowed us to understand the trophic levels of individuals. The two white shark vertebrae showed different isotopic values. The first individual (seven growth layers) presented isotopic ranges from 9.6‰ to 10.8‰ (δ15N) and from -16.5‰ to -13.0‰ (δ13C); this showed a mean ± SD value of 10.3 ± 0.4‰ for δ15N and -14.6 ± 1.3‰ for δ13C. The second individual (five growth layers) presented isotopic ranges from 9.8‰ to 11.1‰ (δ15N) and from -16.9‰ to -15.0‰ (δ13C), displaying a mean ± SD value of 10.8 ± 0.6‰ for δ15N and -15.8 ± 0.8‰ for δ13C. In terms of δ15N values, there were not significant differences (U = 6, p =0.07346) between the two individuals; however, there were significant differences (t = -1.8, p =0.049256) in δ13C values, both at a significance level of 0.05. The absence of differences between the trophic level of the individuals could be related to the trophic level of their preys at the time of age. The differences observed in the case of δ13C are probably correlated to the fact that the first shark was feeding near the coast, while the other feed more offshore.

6707: Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus; GBS) is a zoonotic agent that has a wide range of hosts including both bony and cartilaginous fishes. We describe meningoencephalitis as a result of S. agalactiae (serotype Ia) infection in a female sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus; Nardo, 1827) that stranded on the eastern Mediterranean coast of Israel in 2018. Based on post-mortem examination, histopathology, and bacterial identification, we conclude that this pathogen was the etiologic agent. C. plumbeus is an endangered (EN) species in the Mediterranean Sea according to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red list, with a decreasing number of mature individuals in the population. Information on pathogen prevalence in apex marine predators could inform about potential risks to threatened species and provide indication on the state of the environment in this region. Our findings improve current knowledge about the health status of sharks and warrant further research into the interaction between microbial and high-level organisms in the marine environment.

6708: Pollution of marine organisms by heavy metals can occur by direct contamination via the environment or by ingestion of contaminated preys. In order to monitor ecosystems by apprehending their disturbances, it is important to identify bio-indicator species potentially capable of informing about the quality of the environment in which they live. Some sharks and rays as Mustelus sp., Scyliorhinus canicula (Linné, 1758) and Raja sp. may be used as potentially bioindicators. Closely related and part of the same communities, these species occur in the same habitat, each one occupying a distinct ecological niche whose functioning is defined by competition or by prey-predator system. These cartilaginous fish belong to the characteristic community of Diplodus vulgaris (Sparidae). The Thalassa campaign data were used and related to distribution, species diversity and associated fauna. These results are provided by behavioral studies (abundance, spatial distributions, communities), and monitoring of this bony fish, and are also a first step towards the ecosystem approach to fisheries (EAF).

6709: One of the most abundant and consumed sharks worldwide is the blue shark, Prionace glauca. Due to its high trophic position, it can accumulate large concentrations of potentially toxic elements in its tissues and constitute a risk to human health due to its consumption. As the main route of uptake of trace elements is gastrointestinal, the objective of this study was to determine the biomagnification of mercury (Hg), selenium (Se) and cadmium (Cd) through the main preys of Prionace glauca, on the coast Western Baja California Sur, Mexico. Low average levels of the three trace elements analyzed in the shark muscle tissue were found (Hg = 0.43 ± 0.35 µg g-1 wet weight; Se = 0.53 ± 0.43 µg g-1 dry weight; Cd = 0.24 ± 0.81 µg g-1 wet weight). These values are below the maximum permissible limits so that their meat is suitable for human consumption. Among the female and male individuals no statistically significant differences were found for any of the elements studied. The main prey of the blue shark were the giant squid Dosidicus gigas and the prawn Pleuroncodes planipes, being the latter who provided the greatest contribution of mercury to the blue shark and Dosidicus gigas of selenium. In the case of cadmium, biomagnification did not occur because both preys had higher concentrations of this metal concerning the shark.

6710: Hematology is now a useful diagnostic tool in human and domestic mammalian medicine and is becoming such also in the clinical evaluation of fish. Most of the current knowledge of fish hematology derives from research carried out on agnate organisms like missine and lampreys, on a few species of elasmobranchs and on some species of teleosts, although standardized hematological methods and reference intervals for elasmobranchs have not yet been established. The goal of this research was to compare the number of white blood cells present in the specimens of a population of lesser spotted dogfish (Scyliorhinus canicula) from central Mediterranean Sea with the parasitic charge. 75 sharks were collected in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 12 miles off of Rocchette Punta Ala, in Tuscany. Helminth communities were analyzed in the stomach, spiral valve, liver, gills, mouth and nostrils of all the sharks collected, while hematological analysis has been performed taking blood samples from venous sinus of the cardiac cavity of 32 sharks. Complete blood analysis has been performed for 10 samples, while for the remaining 22 only the leukocyte count was carried out using the fluorescence flow cytometry method. All the hematological parameters were correlated with each other, but just the correlation between the number of white blood cells and parasitic charge for the 32 sharks considered was extremely significant and inversely proportional, as the parasitized sharks showed fewer white blood cells than the not parasitized ones. The possible explanation of this result can be found in the immunosoppression from accumulation of trace elements (Hg, Pb, Cd, Cu, As, Zn) in the tissues of lesser spotted dogfish, as already demonstrated in some studies carried out on green frogs and bony fish.

6711: Elasmobranchs are top-predator organisms, essential to maintain trophic web equilibrium in the marine environment. Therefore, fishery and pollutants represent a real threat for these organisms, besides the high lipid content of their diet makes them bioaccumulators organism. Bioaccumulation was previously studied in liver, gills, gut, but little is known about elasmobranch vertebrae. These are an interesting target to study for their structure. Indeed vertebrae are made up of concentric rings, the external are later formed and the inners are the oldest. For this reason, the vertebrae study could allow to evaluate the correlation between pollutants absorption and life traits. Small-Spotted Catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) was chosen as model because its benthic habits and its ecological importance make it a suitable candidate to study the environmental pollution. Seventy-five specimens were collected in the 'Golfo di Follonica' (Italy). To assess accumulation in vertebrae structure, we analyzed two different parts: the centre and the more external ring. This helped us to denote differences between juvenile and adult stages respectively. Trace element content was assessed through LA-ICP-MS. Results showed a decrease in Pb accumulation during life stages, the same occurred for arsenic and nickel. On the opposite, zinc concentration increases in the external section of vertebra compared to the inner one. This changes could be due to different feeding habits of S. canicula. Indeed, the juveniles feed on small crustaceans and mollusks, organisms known to accumulate arsenic, nickel. On the other hand, adults use to pray fish, with a higher content of Zn. Our data confirm that vertebrae are a reliable marker of pollutant-metals accumulation, and S. canicula is a good candidate for pollution biomonitoring and shark's conservation studies.

6712: Anthropogenic derived contamination is a daily threat to marine resources. Long-living and slow growing, higher trophic level animals like sharks are usually the most affected. Studies have been made to assess the impacts of contamination on sharks, but they mostly rely on very invasive or even lethal sampling. Non-lethal methods must be developed and optimized, with blood and skin biopsies being already used with some success in large endangered animals like cetaceans. This work aimed to assess the potential of skin biopsies to be used as sole tissues in the assessment of metal contamination and biochemical responses in sharks, using the Atlantic lesser-spotted dogfish (Scyliorhinus canicula) as test species. A total of 74 specimens were captured of the shore of Portugal, aboard a commercial trawling vessel, and sampled for skin and muscle once arrived at the lab (in the same day). A total of 13 metals, along with several energy metabolism and oxidative stress related biochemical responses were measured. Overall, skin tissue tended to harbour greater metallic contamination when compared to muscle. However, positive correlations were found between skin and muscle metal levels, across all tested elements. Biochemical responses, mainly energy metabolism related, also seemed to be similarly influenced by the same metal contaminants in both tissues. All correlations and interactions found in-between metals and biomarkers point to a pattern of similar response both in deeper muscle and skin biopsies. Therefore, this work highlights the potential of skin biopsy to be used as substitute for deeper, more invasive (and lethal) muscle sampling. Studies like this one, encompassing comparisons between sub cellular responses to contamination levels in deeper tissues and skin biopsies, are a crucial and most needed step in validating non-lethal methodologies to be used in future efforts to gather ecotoxicological data and to protect larger endangered shark species.

6713: To date, available information on marine litter ingestion in Mediterranean elasmobranchs is still very poor, although these species have an important role in the marine trophic web as predators. This study reports the anthropogenic litter ingestion in four elasmobranch species caught by trawlers and longliners in the southern Tyrrhenian Sea: the lesser-spotted dogfish, Scyliorhinus canicula (n= 27; mean total length TL 40.5 ± 6.3 cm), the velvet belly dogfish, Etmopterus spinax (n= 16; mean TL 21.2 ± 7.7 cm), the blackmouth catshark, Galeus melastomus (n= 12; mean TL 20.7 ± 3.0 cm) and the thornback ray Raja clavata (n= 6; mean TL 65.8 ± 2.8 cm). A total of 61 stomach contents were examined by direct visual sorting at a stereo microscope in order to identify the anthropogenic litter. Once isolated, litter particles were counted and categorized by shape, colour and size. Overall, 18 litter particles were identified from the stomach contents of 14 demersal elasmobranchs (23% of total occurrence, O%). In details, litter items were recorded in seven S. canicula (O%= 25.9), four G. melastomus (O%= 33.3), three R. clavata (O%= 50), whereas no litter ingestion was observed in E. spinax. Transparent and white colours resulted the debris with the highest frequency of ingestion (O%= 25). Fragments were the most common litter in stomachs of both S. canicula (O%= 87.5%) and R. clavata (O%= 75), whereas in G. melastomus fragments and filaments occurred with the same frequency (O%= 50). Most litter particles (55.5% of total debris) had a size less than 5 mm. This is the first time that litter ingestion is observed in R. clavata in Mediterranean waters. Some of these species could be considered as indicators for litter ingestion in marine demersal habitats.

6714: Increasing interest in the management and conservation of elasmobranchs highlights the importance of acquiring further knowledge of their biology and ecology; in this respect, important information can be derived from the analysis of their parasite fauna. Parasitological investigations focused on elasmobranchs from Mediterranean Sea are scarce; the compilation of accurate and updated checklists is further complicated by the occurrence of old records of infection and the doubtful identity of the shark host. A healthy specimen of Common Smoothhound, Mustelus mustelus, (total length: 66 cm) fished as bycatch in northern Adriatic Sea was subjected to a complete parasitological examination. Collected parasites were processed for morphological and morphometric analyses aimed at identifying them to the species level. Parasite identity was confirmed through amplification and sequencing of 28S rDNA. Nematodes belonging to the species Acanthocheilus rotundatus (15 specimens) were recovered from the stomach and the proximal intestine, while cestodes belonging to the species Calliobothrium verticillatum (5 specimens) were collected from the spiral valve. Calliobothrium spp. are known to parasitize different species of Mustelus around the world's oceans. Particularly, C. verticillatum has been reported in M. mustelus from Northeastern Atlantic and only one report dating back to the 50s on this parasite in M. mustelus from Mediterranean Sea exists. Our results would therefore confirm the occurrence of this host-parasite association in Mediterranean waters. Acanthocheilus rotundatus has been described infecting M. mustelus from Adriatic Sea based on morphological evidence; our work provides the first sequence data of A. rotundatus from Mediterranean Sea, since only sequences of specimens collected in extra-Mediterranean areas were available so far. Updated knowledge on the parasite fauna of M. mustelus from Adriatic Sea would contribute to elucidate aspects of the ecology, biology and health status of elasmobranchs from Mediterranean Sea, providing useful information for their proper management and conservation.

6715: Jaws, the novel, was published in 1974 and the film released in 1975. Forty-five years ago, about 800 species of sharks, rays and chimaeras were known to science and the global human population was around 4 billion. Today, about 1,250 chondrichthyan fishes have been described and the human population is roughly 7.5 billion. This presentation reviews the history of shark conservation and management since the 1970s and current challenges faced as the year 2020 approaches.
6716: The advent of Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) technologies has seen a transition from conservation genetics to genomics (from gene to genome scales), which is informing our understanding of species and improving conservation outcomes based on these insights. This technology has provided access to thousands of genome-wide markers, collectively capable of providing reliable inferences about demographic patterns and enabling detection of local adaptation. Examples of applied genomics in elasmobranch conservation and forensics at different levels, from species to individuals are becoming more common as we develop genomic resources for non-model species. For species identification, when diagnostic external morphological characters are lacking, or when identifications rely on body parts, the use of non-expensive techniques such as mtDNA sequencing is often used. However, when dealing with closely related, recently diverged species, as is the case of the Galapagos (Carcharhinus galapagensis) and dusky (C. obscurus) sharks, the combination of mtDNA and genome-wide diagnostic markers is required to distinguish the species. This also allows other biologically relevant patterns of genetic variation to be explored, such as those that arise due to hybridization. A first population connectivity assessment of C. galapagensis in the Eastern Tropical Pacific resulted in the development of 1,873 high-resolution SNP markers. A selected subset of SNPs was further used to successfully assess hybridisation patterns between this, and C. obscurus. Future steps include the use of such markers as forensic tools to develop a cost-effective PCR-based essay to rapidly distinguish the two species from carcases or body parts. Likewise, the development of worldwide genomic resources capable of detecting population structure at large as well as fine geographic scales is crucial at the population level to identify particular signatures of selection and local adaptation that can lead to provenience-detecting markers. Finally, at the individual level the inference of the sex-determination systems in new species is leading the way towards the identification of sex-linked markers that can aid sex identification from fin or tissue samples. Current efforts using in silico and PCR validations are showing that SNP markers can be effective at assigning the correct sex in at least twelve of the sixteen species tested. Applying fundamental knowledge towards the development of molecular traceability tools is the logical and much needed step towards shark conservation.

6717: In the Mediterranean Sea, sharks are currently one of the less frequently observed groups of animals. Scientific surveys do not provide enough observation effort to collect relevant data on the presence and distribution of the species, and fisheries data have been historically scattered and rarely adequate in terms of taxonomic resolution. Following the IUCN regional assessment 57% of the species are listed as endangered and 25 % as still data deficient. New monitoring strategies need to take place in the area to improve data collection, and new technologies can create a link between people and scientists. Data management is crucial in these cases. Here we present sharkPulse, a collaborative international project aiming to involve divers, fishermen, surfers, beachgoers and other ocean users in sharing image-based sightings of sharks. To facilitate users participation the sharkPulse team has developed a web platform (http:\\sharkpulse.org) and a mobile application (IOS and Android). All the data collected are available and shared online with summary tables and distribution maps. To break linguistic barriers and boost participation, the project has created national focal points in several parts of the world (Italy, UK, New Zealand, South Africa, Greece). From 2016, the Italian national focal point has focused his activity on the Mediterranean Sea, collecting more than 900 photographic records of 35 shark species. Here we present a first exploration of these data and highlight some emerging patterns: i) possible identification of strongholds for rare and endangered species; ii) seasonal shifts in pelagic shark distributions; and iii) presence of newborns and immature specimens for broad-ranging species such as the shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) for which these sightings are more frequent (75% of the records) than adults. Integrated collection and analysis of these data can improve scientific understanding of sharks in the Mediterranean Sea, fill the data gap that has historically characterized the basin on these species, and stimulate conservation and recovery actions.

6718: Worldwide, ocean and coastal threat is driven by the rapid expansion of fisheries and global trade markets, whereby overfishing activities and habitat degradation have severely altered elasmobranch populations. The western Indian Ocean is an important conservation area for sharks and rays as this region is a global hotspot for biodiversity and for threatened species. The harvesting of elasmobranchs in this region is amongst others driven by the international shark meat and shark fin trade. In this study, we assessed marine forensics as a tool for complementing traditional identification methods – through the development of a mini-barcoding assay as well as High Resolution Melt (HRM) analysis, relevant to elasmobranch species occurring in the western Indian Ocean region. This involved the testing and optimisation of the standard barcoding region of the cytochrome oxidase c subunit 1 (COI), using traditional barcoding primers as well as two sets of nested PCR primers in a multiplex assay. Preliminary results (only a 22% species identification success rate) indicated the limitations of using only the traditional COI primers and warrented the inclusion of additional gene regions for species identification of future shark forensic cases. In this study, a mini-barcoding multiplex assay comprising three primer sets were optimised and applied to a wide range of shark forensic case studies, involving confiscated shark fins possibly for illegal trade. Furthermore, a HRM approach was validated based on six southern African houndshark species and further optimised for additional commercially exploited species such as hammerhead S. lewini and S. zygaena, copper C. brachyurus, dusky C. obscurus, bull C. leucas, blacktip C. limbatus and blue shark P. glauca. Ultimately, these approaches can be combined to develop a relatively fast and cost-effective identification protocol that can be applied to identify most, if not all, elasmobranch species involved in trade regionally.

6719: Over-exploitation and fishery by-catch leads to an increasing decline of elasmobranchs worlwide; with unpredictable consequences for the health and structure of the ecosystems. According to IUCN, the Mediterranean Sea is amongst the three top regions where the biodiversity of sharks and rays is seriously threatened. Considering the European waters, the IUCN reveals that half of the assessed elasmobranch species, 39 out of 73, are threatened at Mediterranean level. Despite some recent efforts in EU to reduce shark by-catch and mortality (i.e., adoption of the European Commission's Action plan for the Conservation and Management of Sharks, and adoption of the Council Regulation (EU) 2017/127), the EC goals are far from being achieved, and conservation actions need to be set up. Current legislation only prevents retention and trade, but not the actual capture or the mortality that may occur as a result. The factors that contribute to the by-catch and the mortality of elasmobranch during fisheries capture are - in fact - many, but the major is the fishers' attitude. The consciuous and responsible behavior of the employees in commercial fishing activities is fundamental to mitigate the impact of their actions on the marine biodiversity, cartilaginous fishes included. The project eLIFE (elasmobranch low impact fishing experience), has been recently funded by the EU's LIFE programme for the protection of the enviornment. It aims to reduce the elasmobranch by-catch and mortality by promoting best conservation practices in the context of the EU commercial fishing activities in the Mediterranean Sea. It targets several sharks listed as endengered or critically endengered in the Red List of the European marine fishes of the IUCN and it includes the partecipation of 3 EU countries (Italy, Cyprus and Greece). eLIFE is based on the direct involvement of the professional fishers, and will test the efficiency of using low impact fishing gears and correct methods of manipulation for the elasmobranch incidental caught, as well as the use of digital technology, like satellite tags and a smartphone application to monitor the efficency of the conservation actions and to obtain new spatial information.

6720: The Angelshark (Squatina squatina) was once widespread throughout the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, but now is one of the most threatened fish in European waters. Indeed, the angel shark family is identified as the second most threatened elasmobranch taxon after a global review of extinction risk by the IUCN. A unique stronghold remains for the Angelshark in the Canary Islands, but even here the species is under threat. Given the importance of forging bonds with key stakeholders to secure the future of this species, Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI), a collaboration between Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Zoological Society of London and Zoologisches Forschungsmuseum Alexander Koenig, has developed a number of tools to engage interested parties and encourage them to provide information to aid scientific research. Our focus is on the recreational sector, specifically divers and fishers. This year, ASP:CI has re-launched best practice guidelines in collaboration with the recreational fishing sector to a) encourage fishers to safely release any accidentally caught Angelsharks, b) report these encounters and c) gain the trust of the fishing community and raise the awareness on the species. In addition, we completed the first Count the Angels event in Fuerteventura, which brings together dive centres to complete a census of Angelsharks across the island via coordinated diving. A total of 7 dive centres participated, 24 Angelsharks sighted and over 882 diving hours were completed during this event. This not only reinforces the bond with the diving community, but enables greater coverage across large stretches of coastline to better understand Angelshark presence, and in the future, calculate abundance metrics. These tools will ensure and reinforce the bond between scientists and the recreational community, a key task when working with a Critically Endangered species.

6721: Marine megafauna (elasmobranchs, mammals, turtles, birds) is important from an ecological point of view because it occupies upper trophic levels and is also often essential for marine tourism. Species belonging to this group are often heavily impacted by fishing due to their longevity, late sexual maturity and low reproductive output, which affect the capability to recover from depletion. In the Galapagos, marine megafauna is protected throughout the marine reserve and is the main attraction for marine tourism, generating millions of dollars in revenue annually. Multiple artisanal longlining projects were carried out since the 1990s with the aim of redirecting fishing effort from the depleted coastal-demersal species to pelagic fish, such as yellowfin tuna, Thunnus albacares and swordfish, Xiphias gladius. All these projects have resulted in high bycatch of megafauna. Despite its importance in the archipelago, megafauna is still being caught as bycatch in the longline fishery, without independent scientific studies to evaluate its impact, largely due to poor objective definition, data collection, and enforcement. To fill in this knowledge gap, we analyzed data of the fifth longline fishing project (2012-2013) to describe the fishery, identify variables affecting bycatch, and suggest mitigation strategies. This experimental project involved twelve fishing vessels, which deployed 42,007 hooks catching 4,893 individuals belonging to 33 species, mostly yellowfin tuna. Of those, 16 species were protected megafauna, particularly blacktip sharks, Carcharhinus limbatus and oceanic manta, Manta birostris. These species were regularly captured during the two fishing seasons and in all the four bioregions that occur in the archipelago, suggesting little potential to mitigate their catch. As an alternative, we identified 14 hotspots where yellowfin tuna and swordfish could be harvested through more selective fishing techniques. In an archipelago where the main economic activity is marine wildlife tourism, the implementation of an extractive and unselective activity such as pelagic longline fishing should be avoided to ensure the preservation of the Galapagos marine ecosystem and its booming tourism industry.

6722: Fishers have a rich knowledge of the resources and the environment in which they work, that is rarely utilised to provide advice on the status of exploited populations. Fishers "local ecological knowledge" (LEK) can be used to reconstruct species trends, like sharks, that currently are at very low biomass due to overfishing. In this study we used the historical memories of Sicilian fishers to gather data on change in fishing practices and capture of cartilaginous species in the Strait of Sicily over the last decades. We conducted interviews with 27 retired trawl fishers from Mazara del Vallo harbour (SW Sicily) using a pre-defined questionnaire with a series of open and fixed questions and comparing to the present abundance. The questionnaire included specific questions about the trends they perceived in cartilaginous fish occurence abundance between 1940s and 2000s (according to three main time periods 1940-1960, 1961-1980 and 1981-2010), in order to facilitate the estimation of eventual changes over time. A total of 29 species were mentioned by fishermen during interviews, including large pelagic sharks (Carcharhinidae, Sphyrnidae and Lamnidae), mesopredatory demersal sharks (Squalidae, Hexanchidae, Centrophoridae, Oxynotidae, Triakidae, Scyliorhinidae and Squatinidae) and batoids. Overall shark catches were perceived to have diminished since the early 1940s: about 95% of fishers reported the decline of commercially important species (e.g. Mustelus spp.) and indicated species that could have been depleted (e.g. Squatina spp., Sphyrna spp.). Our study shows that LEK of fishers can be beneficial for reconstructing long-term population trends of exploited species when traditional standard data on fisheries catch or species relative abundance from surveys is limited or only available for recent periods. The results obtained cleary indicate the rapid and alarming decline of elasmobranchs in the Strait of Sicily highlighting the need for urgent conservation measures to be adopted.
6723: A growing concern in conserving threatened animals affected by human impact has been significant worldwide. Among marine animals, sawfishes (Chondrichthyes, Pristidae) are considered one of the most endangered families among elasmobranchs, resulting in extinction in many coastal areas around the world, including the Mediterranean Sea. Here, sawfish occurred with two species, Pristis pristis and P. pectinata, until the second half of the last century and are now considered Critically Endangered/Possibly Extinct. The historical occurrence of sawfish in the area is documented by bibliographic/ archival records and numerous preserved historical rostra available in museum collections. In this study we attempted to genetically characterize the historical remains of sawfish from several European museums and to enable, in the future, the preliminary investigation of their evolutionary and ecological relationships with global samples. A total of 80 rostra specimens, dated from 1813 to 1959 and catalogued as unknown origin or Mediterranean (11), were collected from 11 European museums and were properly prepared for ancient DNA genetic analysis. Taxonomic identification at the species level was obtained through PCR amplification of small fragments (150 bp) of two mitochondrial markers commonly used for species identification (i.e., the mitochondrial COI and the NADH2). Sequence comparison with currently available ones from public repositories and phylogenetic tree analyses indicated that the historical specimens belonged to four species, P. pristis, P. zijsron, P. pectinata, and Anoxypristis cuspidata, with a high frequency of mismatches (69%) between molecular identification and species museum cataloguing, when present. These preliminary data also showed the presence of two sequence sub-clusters in the poorly barcoded species P. zijsron. With the expansion of this initial analysis, we will contribute to increase the limited molecular data of these critically endangered large predators and to exploit historical genetic data for reconstructing phylogenetic/phylogeographic extent of the possibly extinct population of Mediterranean sawfish.

6724: Shortfin-mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) and blue shark (Prionace glauca) are the two most captured pelagic shark species in the Atlantic Ocean. Since 1990 Spanish longline fleet has been registered for the highest by-cacth of both species in the Atlantic Ocean. About shortfin-mako, concern has been raised after the last evaluation for the northern Atlantic in 2017 made by ICCAT and the stock assessment update meeting held in 2019. It stated the population being overfished and suffering from overfishing. About blue shark, although capture levels appear to be within sustainable fishing limits, it is subject to high exploitation rates in the Atlantic. Uncertainties in assessment results suggest that additional management actions could be considered for both species. In this study different fisheries management strategies were evaluated for shortfin-mako and blue shark in the Atlantic from the stakeholder’s perspective. Local Ecological Knowledge (LEK) was considered to be useful as fishermen possess a unique knowledge based on their continued interaction with the species and the environment. Information was collected through personal interviews with fishermen from the Spanish longline fleet and surveys sent out to scientists and NGOs. Interviews allowed to collect fishermen’s observations on variations of abundance, distribution patterns, size of capture and seasonal fluctuations for both species. SWOT-analysis was used to study the different factors to be taken into account for various management measures. Main management strategies proposed by stakeholders were time-area closure, especially for blue shark juveniles during the summer months in the Sole Bank, minimum capture size and a quota system. This study suggests that management could be supported by involving stakeholders due to their knowledge about the species and environment. Lastly, observations of fishermen about ecological features of both species could be used as a valid aid for future scientific studies.

6725: Many species of sharks and their relatives are declining worldwide at a rapid rate because of their vulnerable life histories exposed to impacts of fishing and habitat modification. For this reason, they are among the most endangered animals in the ocean. Meanwhile, they are also the most poorly quantified groups of animals in the ocean as basic information on abundance and distribution is lacking for about half of their species. Lack of data is hampering conservation assessment and policy actions and has thus become one of the biggest issues for shark conservation. Available solutions for developing effective conservation actions and reverse loss include exploring alternative sources of information and unconventional methods to collect and analyze abundance and distribution data. Here we show how to transition from data deficient to big data for many shark species. By taking advance of the surge of information on human ocean use and communication, we show how crowdsourcing, web data-mining and machine learning can fill this critical information gap. We integrated these approaches in a modular crowd-sourcing platform that combines social network and web site crawling, web applications, smartphone technology, and image analysis to build the largest database of shark sighting available today. We will show how these data can be used to produce species distribution and models to inform conservation assessments and promote protection and recovery plans.

6726: Thanks to the availability of the MEDITS survey data, a picture of the occurrence, abundance and distribution of Chondrichthyes in the Mediterranean basin was done. During the spring-summer MEDITS period (2012-2015), 41 Chondrichthyes, including 18 sharks (5 Orders and 10 Families), 22 batoids (3 Orders and 4 Families) and 1 chimaera, were detected from several Geographical Subareas (GSAs). In general, it is possible to observe that batoid species had a preferential distribution in the shelf (10-200 m) while “shark” species were more frequent in the slope (200-800 m). Only three species, the Carcharhiniformes Galeus melastomus, Scyliorhinus canicula and the Torpediniformes Torpedo marmorata were caught in all several GSAs studied. On the shelf, the Rajidae family was represented in primis by Raja clavata and then by R. miraletus, R. polystigma and R. asterias. The slope was characterized by the prevalence of the blackmouth catshark G. melastomus in all GSAs followed by S. canicula, E. spinax and Squalus blainville. Throughout a comparison between the maps of trawling fishing pressure in Mediterranean (Sbrana et al., 2013) and our maps of abundance’s species it is clear that the most affected areas, as Adriatic sea and Spanish areas (with the exception of the Baleares islands) registered low abundance of Elasmobranchs but other areas with high level of pressure, as the South western of Sicily, presented high level of abundance, showing that, in this case, other environmental drivers work together with the fishing pressure to define the levels of biomass and density. Results of Generalized Additive Models (GAM) highlighted the depth range (followed by the temperature) as one of the most important drivers influencing the distribution of both batoid and shark species.

6727: Fisheries contribute to food security and poverty alleviation, particularly in developing countries such as Mexico. Therefore, it is important to assess the risks to fisheries resources in a comprehensive way. The vulnerability analysis of 106 species of pelagic, coastal and demersal chondrichthyans in the Gulf of California area performed in this study involves two regions (the southern and entrance), two timescales (2050 and 2099), four types of fishing and eight climate change stressors. The risk from fishing stressors is related to exposure to the demersal prawn fishery, the artisanal fishery, the industrial shark fishery, and the sardine fishery from 2006 to 2017, also depending on the species’ productivity and susceptibility. The risk from climate change stressors was assessed by how species are likely to be affected by eight climate change stressors (rising water temperature, increasing storm frequency and intensity, changing currents and upwelling, increasing salinity, decreasing DO and chlorophyll-a and increasing ocean acidity). The assessment was based on the species’ sensitivity and adaptability to changing habitats and on indicators of what may happen based on IPCC emissions scenarios for the area by 2100. We have assessed which species of chondrichthyans are likely to be highly affected (“Losers”) and those considered “Winners” by assigning each species to six ecological groups (EGs) (a novel and flexible way to allocate a great number of species) based on species’ lifestyle and habitat. The EGs of shelf-inshore, shelf-reef and shelf-sand (≤75 m) are likely to have high exposure risk to the climate change stressors under medium and high emission scenarios, whereas exposure risk from fishing stressors was high for the EGs of shelf-inshore and shelf-sand (≤75 m) in both regions.

6728: The trade of shark-derived products is a primary driver of the decline in shark populations globally. Shark fin is one of China’s top dried seafood products and, with over 80 shark species currently present in the Hong Kong (HK) trade, shark fin soup is an asian delicacy on high demand. The high position of sharks in marine food webs and their relatively long life spans mean that they can often have high concentrations of heavy metals in their tissues. Heavy metals including mercury (Hg), Methylmercury (MeHg), lead (Pb), arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd) and selenium (Se) all have adverse health effects on humans, especially in pregnant women and children. Shark meat contains high values of Hg, often surpassing the recommended human consumption advisory limits. To date, little is known about the risks of consuming shark fin products on a regular basis, and virtually no studies have addressed this issue. Here, we analyze processed shark fins from the China and HK markets (n=267) for Hg, MeHg, Pb, As, Cd and Se to obtain novel information on their heavy metal concentrations and to inform consumers of the risks of ingesting fins from a suite of species (n=9) currently heavily traded. Results indicate all shark species in the study are above maximum consumption Hg limits established by HK and US EPA. A complex of Blacktip species, Carcharhinus longimanus, Prionace glauca, Sphyrna lewini and Sphyrna Zygaena all surpass the European comission’s Hg limits (1ppm) and WHO/JECFA’s MeHg potential tolerable weekly intake (1.6 𝜇gMeHg/kg bw). P. glauca samples were found to surpass inorganic As maximum levels established by WHO/JECFA (70.59% samples > 3 𝜇giAs/kg bw ). Results show high inter and intra-specific variation in Hg, As and MeHg concentrations, as well as low Cd, Se and Pb concentrations for the majority of individuals.

6729: The spiny butterfly ray, Gymnura altavela, is a benthic batoid found on soft bottoms in shallow coastal waters in the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, where it is considered a Critically Endangered species on certain areas of its distribution. As G. altavela is a species with a patchy and discontinuous distribution, the identification, characterization and protection of its congregation areas may be the key issue for the future of the species. Its big size, calmed behaviour and presence in beaches with a high tourist activity make this species an emblematic animal for conservation plans. To evaluate this purpose, a series of monthly surveys were conducted during a year in areas located in Alicante (South-Eastern Spain) with different level of tourism. In each survey, the number of spiny butterfly ray marks found in the sediment with its length, width and location depth were recorded. Live animals found were also measured in length and width, and pictures of the pectoral fins and tail were taken for photoidentification. A total of 26 different alive animals were found during the daily surveys, showing a disc width range of 77-112 cm for males and 53-157 cm for females. The alive specimens found were resting on the bottom covered by sediment beside seagrass meadows of Posidonia oceanica or Cymodocea nodosa. Only juvenile specimens (<64 cm width) were found resting in sand patches within C. nodosa meadows. The occurrence of females was constant throughout the year, while male occurrence was higher in spring. During the period October-June, coinciding with the months of less tourism, spiny butterfly ray specimens and its marks were observed in all the surveyed areas, whereas during June-September period, coinciding with the tourism season, no animals or its marks could be observed in the areas with high level of tourism activities.

6730: As a long-standing citizen science project of the Shark Trust, the Great Eggcase Hunt (GEH) has received nearly a quarter of a million records to date. Initially developed to engage the public in shark conservation and to find out more about the diversity and broad distribution of oviparous elasmobranchs in British waters, the GEH now regularly receives records from around the world, including as far afield as Ecuador. Surprisingly little is known about the distribution and habitat of the spawning and nursery areas of skate and oviparous sharks, and the eggcases of many species have yet to be described. Citizen science engagement can support broader scientific initiatives in areas where data may be otherwise limited and can strengthen inferences made on important habitats. Data obtained from the project so far has allowed us to detail the morphological characteristics of 13 species found around the British Isles, with an additional paper on the distribution of juvenile stages and eggcases of skate in prep. Collaborations with partner organisations - the Dutch Shark Society (Netherlands) and APECE (Portugal) - and the translation of the GEH smartphone app into the corresponding languages has allowed the reach and scope of the project to broaden. The increased accessibility of GEH identification and recording materials has resulted in improved accuracy of submissions of spent eggcases, an increase in submissions of in-situ sightings, and from fish markets, scientific trawls and commercial fisheries. Photographic capabilities within the app have enabled more records to be verified to species level. As the Trust continues to develop the GEH and make it more accessible internationally, our objective is to expand on the existing species-specific knowledge of oviparous elasmobranchs. As a result, this could help inform on the nominal distribution of egg-laying grounds and potentially aid conservation measures on a local and international level.
6731: Social media networks are emerging as an important additional tool for monitoring wildlife especially in areas with low data availability. Libya is located in the central Mediterranean and is considered a data scarce area regarding its marine biodiversity. Few information is also available about elasmobranch species, however this country has been recently identified among the top priority countries for elasmobranch conservation with low conservation likelihood and yet high fisheries pressure. For this work, in the context of an ongoing project, we performed a rapid assessment on social media for detecting elasmobranch occurrences from Libya. A total of 55 records of elasmobranch occurrences collected, with the vast majority (93.73%) resulting from (professional and recreational) fishing activity, while the rest were observations of divers and marine users. All records identified to the species level resulting in fifteen different species but one observation was recorded as Squatina sp. as the identification to the species level was not possible. Carcharhinus plumbeus (≈16%), Glaucostegus cemiculus (≈14%), Squatina squatina (≈10%) and Rhinobatos rhinobatos (≈10%) were the most commonly posted species. The vast majority of the observation depicted fished individuals of which ≈78% species listed Endangered or Critically Endangered in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, while ≈60% were species protected by the Barcelona Convention and consequently Recommendation GFCM/42/2018/2 (amending GFCM/36/2012/3); in both cases, Libya is a signatory party. This is a very first step on a long-term project that aims to understand the elasmobranch diversity in Libya and bring into light information about their fishing and trade. Hereby we present the first data collected through the social media network FacebookTM, however in the near future further observation will be collected and findings will be complemented with fish and auction market surveys and questionnaires to all relevant stakeholders.

6732: Angel sharks (Squatinidae) are considered one of the most threatened Families of chondrichthyans in the world. Of the 22 species, three are present in the Mediterranean – Sawback Angelshark Squatina aculeata, Smoothback Angelshark S. oculata, and Angelshark S. squatina – all three are Critically Endangered. Population sizes and geographic ranges of these species have declined primarily due to overfishing and habitat loss. With angel sharks now rarely encountered, reliance falls on fisheries data, reports of incidental catch, citizen science, social media, and interviews with fishers to increase knowledge on distribution. The Mediterranean has revealed itself to be a hotspot of extinction risk for chondrichthyans. In 2012, the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) banned the retention of 24 species of exceptionally threatened elasmobranchs, including the three species of angel sharks. Although protected on paper, these species remain exposed to fisheries pressure by those coastal states yet to act on their commitments. The complex and multijurisdictional nature of the Mediterranean (with >20 coastal states and territories) creates a need for collaborative action to build capacity for angel shark conservation. Drawing on the expertise of the Angel Shark Conservation Network, a group of regional experts were brought together in Tunisia (in March 2019) to begin development of a Regional Action Plan for these imperiled species. The Action Plan outlines key threats, goals, objectives, and actions needed to achieve the vision that: Mediterranean angel sharks are restored to robust populations, fulfilling their ecological roles in healthy ecosystems. This work follows on from the development of the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Angel Shark Conservation Strategy which provides a framework for improved protection, guiding future research, management, policy and conservation actions.

6733: Food authenticity has received an increasing focus due to high profile cases of mislabeling, with increasing numbers of investigations identifying sales of endangered or prohibited species that were illegally caught or landed under international and/or national legislation. A total of 160 shark products (steaks or fillets) were examined from fishmongers and markets across Greece and Italy from over a decade. Both countries follow food and safety legislation regarding elasmobranch meat sales, which require specific commerial designation on labels - “Galeos” and “Palombo” for Greece and Italy that are restricted to only Mustelus spp.. The barcode (a partial sequence of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I gene, COI) was used to analyze samples, and species were identified by reference to genetic databases (BOLD and GenBank). The results revealed differences in patterns of species utilisation between countries, with Italy showing a higher level of mislabeling and prohibited species in sales. About three quarter of products (73.75%) originated from species that are locally listed as threatened by the IUCN red list (vulnerable, endangered and critically endangered). The mislabeled products represent 57.76% of all sales, and of them, 47.31% originated from species with current prohibitions on landings or CITES listings. This includes large sharks (i.e. H. griseus, H. perlo, A. vulpinus) that bear little resemblance to Mustelus spp. and likely demonstrate deliberate substitution. Mislabeled products are providing a route for prohibited and protected sharks to enter the food supply chain and be sold to consumers who are misguided and unaware they are purchasing endangered species.

6734: Galeorhinus galeus (Linnaeus, 1758) is a demersal shark, belonging to the Galeomorphii superorder and the Triakidae family. A follow-up, carried out in the late nineties, allowed to establish the total length frequencies distributions of 414 individuals. The analysis of size structures allowed determining the growth and exploitation parameters required by the Thompson and Bell model (1934). This model designed for the length-based analysis, evaluates the impact of a variation in fishing effort with mesh change effect in short and long-term catch forecasts. Input data are provided by the Jones technique (1983), which, by pseudo-cohort analysis (VPA), determines mortality coefficients. Changes in fishing mortality F (VPA) show that the smallest classes are the least fished (low F values). Juveniles are not vulnerable to exploitation; this phenomenon partly assures the state of the stock, but do not overshadow the fishing pressure suffered by the parents. Such observation reflects an overexploitation situation, recruitment type. The Thompson and Bell model calculates F-factors and corresponding biomass, Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) and Maximum Sustainable Economic Yield (MSEY). It suggests increasing the current fishing effort at least three times without any collapse risk for the population but without appreciable production gain. This analysis put the last touches on the hypothesis given by the cohort analysis. The results reflect a high vulnerability of the school shark due to its occurrence on the different biotopes. In order to the stock for sustainability, the effort must be transferred to other sea bottoms and reduce current individuals size to 130-140 cm of total length. 6735: The Shortfin Mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) is the world’s fastest shark, and sought for its meat, fins and sport. Overfished and overlooked by fisheries managers for decades, North Atlantic mako are now on the brink of population collapse. Since 2004 Scientific advisors to the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) have warned that the stock was overfished, that overfishing was likely, and that the South Atlantic stock was likely fully exploited. Subsequent ICCAT stock assessments culminated in stark advice in 2017. With evidence for the North Atlantic showing a 90% probability that the stock is overfished and experiencing overfishing, ICCAT scientists recommended the most effective immediate measure: a complete prohibition of retention. Yet despite the clarity of scientific advice Parties to ICCAT adopted a Recommendation which did not cap landings and has failed to stop overfishing. To this day mako sharks remain a No Limits species in high-seas fisheries. In 2019 several publications have furthered the understanding of the plight of mako sharks: updated projections and new scientific advice from ICCAT reinforcing the severity of the population decline; publication of an IUCN Red List reassessment recognising Shortfin Mako as now globally Endangered; and listing proposals for Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) (result pending at the time of writing). In the context that the fleets from the European Union (EU) take more makos than any other ICCAT Party - and with the EU a cosponsor of the 2019 CITES Appendix II listing proposal - this talk will explore the pressing need for management for makos (with an empahisis on the actions of the EU), and consider the opportuntiies for complimentarity between Wildlife Treaties such as CITES and the Regional Fisheries Management Organisations such as ICCAT.
6736: Part of the job as a researcher is to communicate research with the public and make information accessible, but how to do it efficiently can be a challenge. Social media is a great platform for reaching a large amount of people and if handled correctly it can be a very efficient communication tool. There is also a value in being mentioned and talked about by utilizing social media as well as legacy mass communication channels to enrich information exchanges between the scientific community and public audiences about elasmobranch. By using social media effectively for outreach such as interactions with reporters/newspapers and activly participating in discussion on social media, can assist the researchers field by promoting his/her scientific impact. My thesis and guidelines is a great startingpoint for any researcher that wants to use social media for elasmobranch communication. The communication guidelines I created in my Bachelor are based on social media studies, marketing strategies and my own thesis. The Institute of Marine Research used these guidelines in a communication project, to get public citizens to report sightings of basking sharks in Norwegian waters. The basking shark has become a rare sight due to overfishing/low reproductive rate. Due to the rarity of the shark in Norwegian waters it was important that we reached a broad audience. Through The Institute of Marine Research communication channels on social media and traditional outlets such as newspapers/radio our reach went farther than expected and we had an overwhelming positive feedback from the public with a 33% increase of yearly reported observations. From 37 reports over five years, to 21 reports in 1 month. Ultimately this study demonstrates that our communication strategy and social media guidelines are an effective way of research communication and this contribution may be especially relevant for scientists using social media for elasmobranch research communication.

6738: We present on an international expedition for shark research to the Saba Bank in the Dutch Caribbean organised by the Dutch Elasmobranch Society (NEV), the Saba Conservation Foundation (SCF) and the Nature Foundation Sint Maarten (NFSM) in July 2019. Part of this research is learning more about the behaviour of the sharks in and around the traps. Mote Marine lab have developed a video system that can be used to register shark behaviour. This will be combined with a close kin genetics study to help estimate population size. Stress levels in captured sharks: Taking blood samples (lactate, Ph) of captured animals to assess their welfare when handled on board.

6739: Conservation of apex predators is a key challenge both in marine and terrestrial ecosystems, and sharks represent one of the most endangered groups in the ocean as a consequence of fishing exploitation, high vulnerability and a generalized lack of data on ecology and conservation status. This situation is particularly critical in the Mediterranean Sea due to its millenarian history of exploitation. Even if the white shark is a rare but persistent inhabitant of the Mediterranean Sea, its ecology in the area is still largely unknown. We have scarce information about white shark distribution and habitat use, aspects that are critical for conservation and management. The species is currently assessed as “Critically Endangered” according to the IUCN Regional Redlist criteria. In this study, we built the most comprehensive database of white shark occurrence records in the area (773 observations) and used them to characterize the spatial and temporal patterns of abundance of Mediterranean white sharks within a large temporal window (1860-2016). We fitted generalized additive models to standardized occurrence rates and used spatially disaggregated information on human coastal population abundance as a proxy of observation effort. Our results suggest a complex trajectory of population change characterized by a historical increase and a more recent steep reduction (61.5%) since the second half of 20th-century. Declines ranged between 52% and 97% across different Mediterranean sectors, with a contemporary regional contraction of the spatial distribution. For the first time, these results would inform conservation assessments, underlining the importance to produce status assessments based on population trends that are not suspected but quantitatively inferred. Furthermore, our analyses resulted instrumental to advance new hypotheses on the white shark occurrence and ecology in the Mediterranean Sea and to plan tagging programs with the purpose of collecting high-quality ecological data such distribution, population structure, foraging and habitat use.

6740: The biggest threats to batoids (rays and skates) in the Mediterranean are overfishing and bycatch. The protection of these species is challenging, particularly due to inadequate labeling in fishing ports or inadequate fisheries regulations. Small-scale vessels in the Mediterranean make up 83% of the total fishing fleet, being fixed nets (trammel and gill nets) the most common used gear. In the Valencia region (Spanish Mediterranean) trammel nets are the most common (51%). In this fishery batoids are an important element of bycatch, although catch data on these species is scant. The present study aims to: 1) describe the impact of bycatch (CPUE) for batoid species in trammel nets in the Valencia region, 2) address diversity, spatial and seasonal differences in batoids bycatch composition, and 3) identify and propose direct measures to asses this issue on the unreported and unregulated fishing practices in the region. From January to December 2017, both onboard observation on fishing vessels and sampling of catches at the landing site were carried out in three different ports of the Valencian region. In total, 81 sets from 14 vessels were monitored, giving a record of 429 batoid specimens of 12 different species and five families (Dasyatidae, Gymnuridae, Myliobatidae, Rajidae and Torpedinidae). The most abundant were Torpedo marmorata (25,8%; total average), Torpedo torpedo (25,4%) and Raja radula (16,3%). All the catches were discarded, sold privately or sold at market without identification at species level. There was not significant correlation between batoid’s size and the panel mesh size of trammel nets. Data collected showed seasonal differences in size and total biomass, with a higher rate of captures of larger specimens during the period from March to June. Our results highlight the need of further studies in the area and future implementation of mitigation measures, such as adequate reporting of catches.

6741: The Mediterranean Sea is considered as one of the most dangerous places for sharks and rays in the world, with more than 50% of its species under risk of extinction. Fisheries bycatch is the main threat to sharks and rays in the region. Full evaluation of fisheries impact on shark populations, however, is hampered i.a. by the lack of data on post-release survival rates, highly dependent on fishing strategy and handling practices during the release of the animal, and on key nursery areas and migration routes. Proper monitoring programs are lacking in the majority of Mediterranean countries. Existing bycatch recording systems, including paper based and electronic fisheries logbooks as well as voluntary reporting tools developed by citizen science initiatives, often lack harmonization and interoperability and frequently show weak sustainability and user ownership. Furthermore, fishers and often also port authorities lack capacity to identify protected species and are not aware of legislation and procedures for landing and marketing. The SafeSharks project focuses on the Southern Adriatic adopting a comprehensive approach including 1) stakeholder engagement to raise awareness of the fishing sector on shark status and create ownership to the issue, 2) roundtables of relevant actors (scientists, seafood market and fishing sector, NGOS, authorities) to address key needs in order to improve monitoring, control and surveillance of sharks bycatch and facilitate collaboration, 3) satellite tagging to assess post release survival rates and establishment best handling and release practices and 4) seafood fraud risk assessment in the main Italian markets linked to the Southern Adriatic. Preliminary results of the project will be presented, together with the outcomes of the workshop “A Mediterranean where sharks, rays, skates, and chimeras are valued and managed for sustainability: From Citizen science to implementation of regulation for bycatch of vulnerable sharks and rays in the Mediterranean”.

6742: An increasing onus on tropical elasmobranch management has revealed a paucity in data on abundance, distribution and fisheries. The Republic of Cabo Verde is drafting their national plan of action for sharks, and a lack of coastal fisheries dependent and independent information on elasmobranchs necessitates the creation of a baseline. We combined baited remote underwater video (BRUV) and interviews with traditional fishermen to create the first assessment of the diversity, distribution, and fisheries involvement of elasmobranchs around the eastern islands of Sal, Boavista and Maio, including the remote offshore reef João Valente. Over 200 hours of footage revealed 216 elasmobranchs spanning 16 species from 6 taxonomic families. Three findings were particularly notable: i) CPUE was highest in Maio, the island with the smallest human population; ii) Carcharhinidae spp. were observed in considerably greater abundance in Sal, followed by Boavista; meanwhile Maio and João Valente displayed an absence of large-bodied Carcharhinids; iii) Species richness was consistent across islands, with Boavista and Sal recorded diversity. Results from 207 fisher interviews revealed that 88% of fishers fished sharks, with endangered scalloped hammerheads cited as the most widely captured species. Most fishers (95%) noted a decline in marine resources over the past 5-10 years, with 70% perceiving significant reductions in sharks captured. Cabo Verde’s eastern islands hosts high relative diversity and abundance of coastal elasmobranchs compared to West Africa; higher trophic level species show evidence of intensive exploitation notably with increasing proximity to the capital city Praia. Results of this study are conservative: although fishers interviewed were anonymous and care was taken with the structure and delivery of survey questions, fishers were often reluctant to share information as many believe elasmobranch fisheries to be illegal. Nonetheless, our study suggests that artisanal and semi-industrial fisheries are strongly impacting coastal shark populations.

6743: To document the rapidly declining abundance of Turkish marine resources, a timeline of commercial fisheries extinctions and a list of threatened or extirpated marine species are presented for the Black Sea and Sea of Marmara for Turkey. Turkish nationally reported fisheries data were compared over a 50 year period from 1967 (the first year data were spatially allocated) to 2016 to assess which species are now extirpated (i.e., currently completely absent from the reported catch data), and which species have become commercially extinct (i.e., whose catch declined by 75-99.9%). Other important taxa, with special attention paid to sharks not captured by the statistics, are discussed using accounts from peer-reviewed literature, grey-literature and personal accounts from local scientist and fishers. The Black Sea has 25 extirpated species and 19 commercially extinct marine species, while the Sea of Marmara has 22 extirpated species and 32 commercially extinct species. We interpret these extinctions and declines as indications of potential ecosystem collapses and urge management to be more effective in rebuilding the Turkish marine fisheries, before it becomes too late.

6744: Coastal ecosystems are highly affected by elevated fishing pressure, targeting a higher number of species in continental waters and being sharks and rays among the most disturbed and harvested species. The increasing demand for shark fins and meat in combination with by-catch captures has led shark populations all over the world to an alarming decline. The Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) represents an optimal opportunity to serve as a case study for shark conservation, carrying the potential for worldwide implications. However, the lack of information is still a key problem for the establishment of definitive conservation and management policies. The largest part of elasmobranch landings from artisanal fisheries are juvenile sharks; captured sharks are landed finless, decapitated, and ready to be processed. These, together with the lack of taxonomic knowledge from fisherman and fisheries control agents, make proper identification a challenging task. Therefore, the use of genetic tools for the identification of the shark species is crucial, due to the high observed abundance of juvenile sharks collected, the presence of cryptic species and important genetic population units that might probe essential for conservation and establishment of baselines for further shark research in the ETP. Here, we present barcoding and genetic diversity results from the mitochondrial NADH2 gene used for the identification of 12 species from shark landings in the Northern Colombian Pacific region (ETP) from 2016 to 2018. Two species categorized as threatened under the IUCN Red List, Sphyrna lewini (Endangered) and Carcharhinus falciformis (Vulnerable) occurred frequently in the samples analyzed (21% and 18%, respectively). Our findings are of great importance, particularly for threatened species, as the genetic diversity results showed low values compared to other species in the study. This study is the baseline for further research in the area aiming for understanding shark population dynamics, connectivity between populations as well as the identification of nursery areas.
